# Chapter 42: The Recommendation Engine

## 42.1 The RecommendationEngine Struct

```rust
pub struct RecommendationEngine {
    pub db: PgPool,
}

impl RecommendationEngine {
    pub fn new(pool: PgPool) -> Self {
        Self { db: pool }
    }
}
```

## 42.2 Getting Recommendations

The engine first checks a precomputed cache, then falls back to live computation:

```rust
pub async fn get_recommendations(
    &self,
    query: &RecQuery,
    config: &Config,
) -> Result<Vec<RecResult>, AppError> {
    let limit = query.n.min(config.rec_max_recommendations);
    if limit == 0 {
        return Ok(Vec::new());
    }

    // 1. Check precomputed cache
    let cached = check_cache(&self.db, query, config, limit).await?;
    if !cached.is_empty() {
        return Ok(cached);
    }

    // 2. Compute live
    compute_live(&self.db, query, config, limit).await
}
```

## 42.3 Live Computation

The live computation is the heart of the recommendation engine:

```rust
async fn compute_live(
    db: &PgPool,
    query: &RecQuery,
    config: &Config,
    limit: usize,
) -> Result<Vec<RecResult>, AppError> {
    // 1. Get seed metadata
    let seed = sqlx::query_as::<_, (i32, String, String)>(...)
        .bind(&query.url_id)
        .fetch_optional(db)
        .await?
        .ok_or_else(|| AppError::NotFound(...))?;

    // 2. Get co-occurrence candidates
    let cooccur: Vec<CooccurRow> = sqlx::query_as::<_, CooccurRow>(...)
        .bind(&query.url_id)
        .bind(limit as i64)
        .fetch_all(db)
        .await?;

    // 3. Get tag fallback candidates (if needed)
    let use_tag_fallback = favouriter_count < config.rec_min_favouriters_for_collab as i32;
    let tag_candidates = if use_tag_fallback {
        fetch_tag_candidates(db, &query.url_id, &seed_title, &seed_author, limit).await?
    } else {
        Vec::new()
    };

    // 4. Merge and score candidates
    let mut scored: HashMap<String, CandidateScore> = HashMap::new();
    // ... merge co-occurrence and tag candidates

    // 5. Apply community voting boost
    let net_votes = get_community_votes(db, &candidates).await?;
    // ... apply boost formula

    // 6. Sort and take top N
    candidates.sort_by(|a, b| b.score.partial_cmp(&a.score).unwrap_or(...));
    let top: Vec<CandidateScore> = candidates.into_iter().take(limit).collect();

    // 7. Fetch metadata for results
    // ...

    Ok(results)
}
```

## 42.4 Precomputation

For popular stories, recommendations can be precomputed and cached in the database:

```rust
pub async fn compute_and_cache(
    &self,
    url_id: &str,
    config: &Config,
) -> Result<(), AppError> {
    let results = compute_live(&self.db, &query, config, ...).await?;

    // Clear old cache entries
    sqlx::query("DELETE FROM precomputed_recommendations WHERE url_id = $1")
        .bind(url_id)
        .execute(&self.db)
        .await?;

    // Insert new entries
    for (rank, result) in results.iter().enumerate() {
        sqlx::query(
            r#"INSERT INTO precomputed_recommendations
               (url_id, recommended_url_id, score, rank, computed_at)
               VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, NOW())"#,
        )
        .bind(url_id)
        .bind(&result.url_id)
        .bind(result.score as f32)
        .bind(rank as i16)
        .execute(&self.db)
        .await?;
    }

    Ok(())
}
```

# Chapter 43: The Collection Worker

## 43.1 What is the Collection Worker?

The collection worker is a background process that scrapes user favourites from fanfiction sites and builds the co-occurrence data needed for recommendations.

Think of it as a librarian who walks through the library, noting which books are on the same shelves as which other books.

## 43.2 The SiteFetcher Trait

Each site implements the `SiteFetcher` trait:

```rust
#[async_trait]
pub trait SiteFetcher: Send + Sync {
    fn site_domain(&self) -> &str;

    async fn collect_favouriters(
        &self, client: &Client, work_url: &str, max_pages: u32,
    ) -> Result<Vec<String>, ScrapeError>;

    async fn collect_user_favourites(
        &self, client: &Client, user_url: &str, max_pages: u32,
    ) -> Result<Vec<String>, ScrapeError>;

    fn user_hash(&self, user_url: &str) -> String {
        let mut hasher = Sha256::new();
        hasher.update(user_url.to_lowercase().as_bytes());
        hex::encode(hasher.finalize())
    }
}
```

## 43.3 The Collection Queue

The worker uses a Redis list as a job queue:

```rust
pub async fn enqueue(
    &self,
    url_id: &str,
    site_domain: &str,
    site_work_id: &str,
) -> Result<(), redis::RedisError> {
    let item = QueueItem {
        url_id: url_id.to_string(),
        site_domain: site_domain.to_string(),
        site_work_id: site_work_id.to_string(),
    };
    let json = serde_json::to_string(&item)?;
    let key = format!("collection_queue:{}", site_domain);
    // ...
}
```

## 43.4 The Worker Loop

```rust
pub async fn run(&self) {
    info!("Collection worker started");

    loop {
        for fetcher in &self.fetchers {
            let domain = fetcher.site_domain();
            let key = format!("collection_queue:{}", domain);

            let item_str: Option<String> = {
                let mut conn = self.redis.lock().await;
                redis::cmd("LPOP").arg(&key).query_async(&mut *conn).await.unwrap_or(None)
            };

            if let Some(item_str) = item_str {
                // Apply rate limit
                if let Some(rl) = self.rate_limiters.get(domain) {
                    rl.wait_if_needed().await;
                }

                match serde_json::from_str::<QueueItem>(&item_str) {
                    Ok(item) => {
                        if let Err(e) = self.process_work(item).await {
                            error!("Error processing work on {}: {}", domain, e);
                        }
                    }
                    Err(e) => warn!("Invalid queue item: {}", e),
                }
            }
        }

        // Brief sleep to avoid busy-looping
        tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(100)).await;
    }
}
```

## 43.5 Processing a Work

The `process_work` method:
1. Fetches the list of users who favourited the story
2. For each new user, fetches their favourite works
3. Updates the co-occurrence table for each pair of favourited works
4. Updates the favouriter count

This builds the data foundation that the recommendation engine uses.

```rust
pub async fn suggest_handler(
    State(state): State<Arc<AppState>>,
    Json(body): Json<SuggestBody>,
) -> Result<Json<Value>, AppError> {
    // Resolve the suggested URL
    let scraper = state.scraper_registry.find_scraper(&body.suggested_url)
        .ok_or_else(|| AppError::BadRequest(-5, format!("unsupported URL")))?;
    let meta = scraper.lookup(&state.http_client, &body.suggested_url).await?;
    let suggested_url_id = meta.url_id;

    // Validate both fics exist
    // ... enqueue for collection if not

    // Submit the suggestion
    let suggestion_id = submit_suggestion(
        &state.db, &body.url_id, &suggested_url_id, "0.0.0.0", body.comment.as_deref(),
    ).await?;

    Ok(Json(json!({"err": 0, "suggestion_id": suggestion_id})))
}
```

## 44.2 Voting on Suggestions

```rust
pub async fn vote_handler(
    State(state): State<Arc<AppState>>,
    Json(body): Json<VoteBody>,
) -> Result<Json<Value>, AppError> {
    if body.vote != 1 && body.vote != -1 {
        return Ok(Json(json!({"err": -1, "msg": "vote must be 1 or -1"})));
    }

    let new_score = cast_vote(&state.db, body.suggestion_id, "0.0.0.0", body.vote as i16).await?;

    Ok(Json(json!({"err": 0, "new_score": new_score})))
}
```

# Part X: Advanced Search

# Chapter 45: PostgreSQL Full-Text Search

## 45.1 What is Full-Text Search?

Full-text search (FTS) allows you to search through text content using natural language queries. Unlike simple `LIKE '%keyword%'` searches, FTS:

- Understands word stemming ("running" matches "run")
- Handles stop words ("the", "a", "is" are ignored)
- Supports ranking by relevance
- Can search across multiple columns

## 45.2 FicHub's Text Search Column

FicHub adds a `tsvector` column to `fic_info`:

```sql
ALTER TABLE fic_info ADD COLUMN text_search tsvector;

CREATE INDEX idx_fic_info_text_search ON fic_info USING gin(text_search);
```

The `tsvector` is a pre-processed representation of the text that makes searching fast.

## 45.3 The GIN Index

A GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) index makes text searches very fast. Without it, every search would need to scan the entire table. With a GIN index, PostgreSQL can find matching documents almost instantly.

## 45.4 Automatic Updates with Triggers

FicHub uses a PostgreSQL trigger to keep the search column up to date:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION update_fic_info_text_search() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
    NEW.text_search :=
        setweight(to_tsvector('english', COALESCE(NEW.title, '')), 'A') ||
        setweight(to_tsvector('english', COALESCE(NEW.author, '')), 'B') ||
        setweight(to_tsvector('english', COALESCE(NEW.description, '')), 'C');
    RETURN NEW;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;
```

The `setweight` function assigns different weights:
- **A** (title): Highest relevance
- **B** (author): Medium relevance
- **C** (description): Lower relevance

## 45.5 Searching

To search, FicHub uses the `plainto_tsquery` function:

```sql
SELECT *, ts_rank(text_search, plainto_tsquery('english', 'harry potter')) AS rank
FROM fic_info
WHERE text_search @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'harry potter')
ORDER BY rank DESC;
```

The `@@` operator checks if the search query matches the document, and `ts_rank` computes a relevance score.

---

# Chapter 46: The Search Query Builder

## 46.1 Dynamic Query Building

FicHub's search supports many filters (tags, word count, completion status, date range, etc.). Building these dynamically requires careful SQL construction.

## 46.2 The SearchQueryBuilder

```rust
pub struct SearchQueryBuilder {
    pub params: SearchParams,
    hidden_threshold: i16,
}

impl SearchQueryBuilder {
    pub fn build_data_query(&self) -> QueryBuilder<Postgres> {
        let has_q = self.params.q.is_some();

        let mut qb = QueryBuilder::<Postgres>::new("SELECT fi.*, ");

        if let Some(ref q) = self.params.q {
            qb.push("ts_rank(fi.text_search, plainto_tsquery('english', ");
            qb.push_bind(q);
            qb.push(")) AS rank FROM fic_info fi WHERE 1=1");
        } else {
            qb.push("NULL::real AS rank FROM fic_info fi WHERE 1=1");
        }

        self.push_where_clauses(&mut qb);

        // ORDER BY
        let sort = self.params.sort.as_deref().unwrap_or(
            if has_q { "-relevance" } else { "-date" },
        );

        qb.push(" ORDER BY ");
        match sort {
            "-relevance" => qb.push("rank DESC"),
            "-date" => qb.push("fi.fic_updated DESC"),
            "-words" => qb.push("fi.words DESC"),
            "-chapters" => qb.push("fi.chapters DESC"),
            "-title" => qb.push("fi.title ASC"),
            _ => qb.push("fi.fic_updated DESC"),
        }

        // LIMIT / OFFSET
        let page = self.params.page.unwrap_or(1).max(1);
        let per_page = self.params.per_page.unwrap_or(20).max(1);
        let offset = (page - 1) * per_page;
        qb.push(" LIMIT ");
        qb.push_bind(per_page as i64);
        qb.push(" OFFSET ");
        qb.push_bind(offset as i64);

        qb
    }
}
```

## 46.3 The SQLx QueryBuilder

SQLx's `QueryBuilder` makes it safe to build dynamic queries:

```rust
fn push_where_clauses(&self, qb: &mut QueryBuilder<Postgres>) {
    // Full-text search
    if let Some(ref q) = self.params.q {
        qb.push(" AND fi.text_search @@ plainto_tsquery('english', ");
        qb.push_bind(q);
        qb.push(")");
    }

    // include_tags — ALL must match
    for tag in &self.params.include_tags {
        qb.push(" AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fic_tags ft");
        qb.push(" JOIN tags t ON t.id = ft.tag_id");
        qb.push(" WHERE ft.url_id = fi.id");
        qb.push(" AND t.name = ");
        qb.push_bind(&tag.tag_name);
        qb.push(" AND t.tag_type_id = ");
        qb.push_bind(tag.tag_type_id);
        qb.push(" AND ft.score >= ");
        qb.push_bind(self.hidden_threshold);
        qb.push(")");
    }

    // ... more filters
}
```

Each `push_bind` safely adds a parameterized value, preventing SQL injection.

---

# Chapter 47: Tag Filters in Search

## 47.1 Three Types of Tag Filters

FicHub supports three types of tag-based filtering:

### Include All (AND)

```rust
for tag in &self.params.include_tags {
    qb.push(" AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fic_tags ft");
    qb.push(" JOIN tags t ON t.id = ft.tag_id");
    qb.push(" WHERE ft.url_id = fi.id");
    qb.push(" AND t.name = ");
    qb.push_bind(&tag.tag_name);
    qb.push(" AND t.tag_type_id = ");
    qb.push_bind(tag.tag_type_id);
    qb.push(")");
}
```

"Find stories that have ALL of these tags."

### Exclude (AND NOT)

```rust
for tag in &self.params.exclude_tags {
    qb.push(" AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fic_tags ft");
    // ... similar to include
    qb.push(")");
}
```

"Find stories that have NONE of these tags."

### Include Any (OR)

```rust
if !self.params.include_any_tags.is_empty() {
    qb.push(" AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fic_tags ft");
    qb.push(" JOIN tags t ON t.id = ft.tag_id");
    qb.push(" WHERE ft.url_id = fi.id");
    qb.push(" AND (");
    let mut first = true;
    for tag in &self.params.include_any_tags {
        if !first { qb.push(" OR"); }
        first = false;
        qb.push(" (t.name = ");
        qb.push_bind(&tag.tag_name);
        qb.push(" AND t.tag_type_id = ");
        qb.push_bind(tag.tag_type_id);
        qb.push(")");
    }
    qb.push("))");
}
```

"Find stories that have AT LEAST ONE of these tags."

## 47.2 Tag Filter Syntax

Tag filters use a comma-separated format:

```
include_tags=1:Harry Potter,2:Hermione Granger
```

Where `1` is the tag type ID and `Harry Potter` is the tag name.

```rust
pub fn parse_tag_filters(input: &str) -> Result<Vec<TagFilter>, String> {
    let mut filters = Vec::new();
    for part in input.split(',') {
        let part = part.trim();
        if part.is_empty() { continue; }
        let colon_pos = part.find(':').ok_or_else(|| {
            format!("Invalid tag filter format '{}': expected 'type_id:name'", part)
        })?;
        let type_id: i16 = part[..colon_pos].parse()
            .map_err(|e| format!("Invalid tag type_id: {}", e))?;
        let name = part[colon_pos + 1..].to_string();
        filters.push(TagFilter { tag_type_id: type_id, tag_name: name });
    }
    Ok(filters)
}
```

# Chapter 48: What is OPDS?

## 48.1 Open Publication Distribution System

OPDS (Open Publication Distribution System) is a standard for publishing and distributing e-books. It allows e-readers (like Kindle, Kobo, and Calibre) to browse and download books from online catalogs.

## 48.2 How OPDS Works

1. The e-reader connects to an OPDS catalog URL
2. The server returns an XML feed listing available books
3. The e-reader displays the list to the user
4. When the user selects a book, the e-reader downloads it

## 48.3 OPDS Feeds

OPDS feeds are XML documents that list books with metadata:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<feed xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom">
  <title>FicHub Catalog</title>
  <link href="https://fichub.net/opds" rel="self"/>
  <entry>
    <title>My Amazing Story</title>
    <author><name>Jane Doe</name></author>
    <link href="https://fichub.net/cache/epub/abc123" rel="alternate"/>
    <content type="text">A great story about...</content>
  </entry>
</feed>
```

## 48.4 FicHub's OPDS Routes

FicHub provides a comprehensive OPDS catalog:

| Route | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `/opds` | Root catalog (entry point) |
| `/opds/new` | Recently added stories |
| `/opds/popular` | Most popular stories |
| `/opds/tags` | Browse by tag type |
| `/opds/tags/{type}` | Tags of a specific type |
| `/opds/tags/{type}/{name}` | Stories with a specific tag |
| `/opds/authors` | Browse by author |
| `/opds/search` | Search the catalog |
| `/opds/shelves` | User shelves (authenticated) |
| `/opds/recommendations` | Recommended stories |

```rust
pub async fn root_catalog() -> impl IntoResponse {

<feed xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom"
      xmlns:opds="http://opds-spec.org/2010/catalog">
    <title>FicHub Catalog</title>
    <link href="https://fichub.net/opds" rel="self" type="application/atom+xml;profile=opds-catalog"/>
    <link href="https://fichub.net/opds" rel="start" type="application/atom+xml;profile=opds-catalog"/>
    <updated>2024-01-15T10:00:00Z</updated>
    <entry>
        <title>Recently Added</title>
        <link href="/opds/new" rel="subsection" type="application/atom+xml;profile=opds-catalog"/>
        <id>urn:fichub:opds:new</id>
    </entry>
    <entry>
        <title>Popular</title>
        <link href="/opds/popular" rel="subsection" type="application/atom+xml;profile=opds-catalog"/>
        <id>urn:fichub:opds:popular</id>
    </entry>
    <entry>
        <title>Browse by Tag</title>
        <link href="/opds/tags" rel="subsection" type="application/atom+xml;profile=opds-catalog"/>
        <id>urn:fichub:opds:tags</id>
    </entry>
    <entry>
        <title>Search</title>
        <link href="/opds/search" rel="search" type="application/opensearchdescription+xml"/>
        <id>urn:fichub:opds:search</id>
    </entry>
</feed>"#;

    )
}
```

## 49.2 OPDS Authentication

Some OPDS features (like shelves) require authentication. FicHub uses a shared token:

```rust
pub async fn shelf_list(
    State(state): State<Arc<AppState>>,
    headers: HeaderMap,
) -> Result<XmlResponse, AppError> {
    let auth_header = headers.get("Authorization")
        .and_then(|v| v.to_str().ok());

    match auth_header {
        Some(token) if token == format!("Bearer {}", state.config.opds_shelf_token) => {
            // Authorized — show shelves
            // ...
        }
        _ => {
            // Unauthorized — return 401
            // ...
        }
    }
}
```

# Chapter 52: Frontend Integration

## 52.1 Serving the Frontend

FicHub serves a SvelteKit single-page application (SPA) as its frontend:

```rust
.fallback_service(
    ServeDir::new(&frontend_dir)
        .append_index_html_on_directories(true)
        .fallback(ServeFile::new(frontend_dir.join("index.html"))),
)
```

## 52.2 The SPA Pattern

In a SPA, the server always returns the same HTML file, and JavaScript handles routing:

1. User visits `https://fichub.net/search`
2. Server returns `index.html` (since there is no physical `/search` file)
3. JavaScript reads the URL and renders the search page
4. JavaScript makes API calls to `/api/v0/search` for data

## 52.3 CORS

The `CorsLayer::permissive()` allows the frontend to make API requests from any origin. In production, you would restrict this to your specific domain.

## 53.3 Test Patterns Used in FicHub

### The EnvGuard Pattern

Tests that modify environment variables use `EnvGuard` to ensure cleanup:

```rust
struct EnvGuard { keys: Vec<String> }
impl Drop for EnvGuard {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        for key in &self.keys {
            unsafe { std::env::remove_var(key); }
        }
    }
}
```

### The Mutex Lock Pattern

Tests that modify shared state use a mutex to prevent concurrent access:

```rust
static ENV_LOCK: Mutex<()> = Mutex::new(());

#[test]
fn test_something() {
    let _lock = ENV_LOCK.lock().unwrap();
    // ... test code
}
```

# Advanced Topics

# Chapter 55: Async Patterns in Rust

## 55.1 What is Async/Await?

Async/await is Rust's way of writing asynchronous code that looks like synchronous code. Instead of blocking while waiting for I/O, the program can do other work.

```rust
// Synchronous (blocking):
let response = reqwest::get(url).await; // Blocks here

// Asynchronous (non-blocking):
let response = reqwest::get(url).await; // Suspends, allows other work
```

## 55.2 Futures

A `Future` in Rust represents a value that will be available later:

```rust
async fn fetch_data() -> String {
    // This function returns a Future<String>
    "data".to_string()
}
```

When you call `fetch_data()`, it does not immediately return "data". Instead, it returns a `Future` that, when `.await`ed, will produce "data".

## 55.3 The Tokio Runtime

Tokio is the async runtime that executes futures. It provides:

- **Task scheduling**: Running many futures concurrently
- **I/O operations**: Non-blocking network and file operations
- **Timers**: `tokio::time::sleep`
- **Channels**: Communication between tasks

## 55.4 Common Async Patterns in FicHub

### Sequential I/O

```rust
// One after the other
let meta = scraper.lookup(&client, url).await?;
let chapters = scraper.fetch_chapters(&client, &meta).await?;
```

### Concurrent I/O

```rust
// Multiple requests at the same time
let (meta_result, tags_result) = tokio::join!(
    scraper.lookup(&client, url),
    scraper.extract_tags(&client, url),
);
```

### Select

```rust
// Race two operations, use the first to complete
tokio::select! {
    result = long_operation() => handle_result(result),
    _ = tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_secs(30)) => {
        tracing::warn!("Operation timed out");
    }
}
```

### Spawning Tasks

```rust
// Run a task in the background
tokio::spawn(async move {
    // This runs concurrently with the main task
    process_background_job().await;
});
```

## 55.5 Common Pitfalls

### Holding Locks Across .await

```rust
// BAD: Lock is held across .await
let data = lock.lock().await;
some_async_operation().await;  // Lock still held!
drop(data);

// GOOD: Release lock before .await
{
    let data = lock.lock().await;
    // Use data
}  // Lock released here
some_async_operation().await;
```

### Deadlocks

```rust
// BAD: Two tasks waiting for each other
// Task 1: lock A, then lock B
// Task 2: lock B, then lock A

// GOOD: Always acquire locks in the same order
// Both tasks: lock A, then lock B
```

---

# Chapter 56: Database Performance

## 56.1 Indexing

Indexes are like a book's table of contents — they help the database find data without scanning every row.

```sql
-- Index on the primary key (automatically created)
-- fic_info(id) — already indexed

-- Index for full-text search
CREATE INDEX idx_fic_info_text_search ON fic_info USING gin(text_search);

-- Index for author lookups
CREATE INDEX idx_fic_info_author ON fic_info(author);

-- Composite index for tag queries
CREATE INDEX idx_fic_tags_url_tag ON fic_tags(url_id, tag_id);
```

## 56.2 Query Analysis

PostgreSQL provides tools to analyze query performance:

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM fic_info WHERE author = 'Jane Doe';
```

This shows:
- The query plan (which indexes are used)
- Estimated vs. actual rows
- Execution time

## 56.3 Connection Pool Tuning

The connection pool size should match your workload:

- **Read-heavy**: More connections (each query is fast)
- **Write-heavy**: Fewer connections (writes take longer)
- **Mixed**: Balance between the two

FicHub uses 20 connections, which works well for its read-heavy workload.

## 56.4 N+1 Query Problem

The N+1 problem occurs when you fetch N items and then make N separate queries for related data. FicHub avoids this with batch queries:

```rust
// BAD: N+1 queries
for row in &rows {
    let tags = sqlx::query("SELECT * FROM fic_tags WHERE url_id = $1")
        .bind(&row.id)
        .fetch_all(&pool)
        .await?;
}

// GOOD: Single batch query
let url_ids: Vec<&str> = rows.iter().map(|r| r.id.as_str()).collect();
let all_tags = sqlx::query("SELECT * FROM fic_tags WHERE url_id = ANY($1)")
    .bind(&url_ids)
    .fetch_all(&pool)
    .await?;
```

# Chapter 57: Security Best Practices

## 57.1 SQL Injection Prevention

FicHub uses parameterized queries everywhere:

```rust
// SAFE: Parameterized
sqlx::query("SELECT * FROM fic_info WHERE id = $1")
    .bind(user_input)
    .fetch_one(&pool)
    .await?;

// NEVER: String interpolation
let query = format!("SELECT * FROM fic_info WHERE id = '{}'", user_input);
```

## 57.2 XSS Prevention

HTML content is escaped before insertion:

```rust
fn escape_html(s: &str) -> String {
    s.replace('&', "&amp;")
        .replace('<', "&lt;")
        .replace('>', "&gt;")
        .replace('"', "&quot;")
        .replace('\'', "&#39;")
}
```

## 57.3 Rate Limiting

The token bucket rate limiter prevents abuse:

```rust
// Check rate limit before processing
check_tag_rate_limit(&mut redis, "submit", ip, limit).await?;
```

## 57.4 Error Information Leakage

Internal errors are logged but not sent to users:

```rust
AppError::Internal(msg) => {
    tracing::error!("Internal error: {}", msg);  // Logged
    (StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR,
     json!({"err": -1, "msg": "internal server error"}))  // Generic message
}
```

## 57.5 Cache Hash Validation

Download URLs include MD5 hashes to prevent unauthorized access:

```
/cache/epub/abc123?h=def456
```

The server verifies the hash matches the actual file before serving it.

## 58.1 Logging

Every significant event is logged:

```rust
tracing::info!("Starting fichub-rs server on port {}", config.app_port);
tracing::info!("Registered {} scrapers", registry.scraper_count());
tracing::info!("Database migrations applied");
tracing::debug!("Extracted {} tags for {}", tags.len(), url_id);
tracing::warn!("Rate limit exceeded for IP {}", ip);
tracing::error!("Internal error: {}", msg);
```

## 58.2 Request Timing

The TraceLayer logs every request with timing:

```
INFO request{method=GET uri=/api/v0/epub}: response{status=200}: completed in 234ms
```

## 58.3 Metrics to Monitor

Key metrics to watch in production:

| Metric | What It Tells You |
|--------|-------------------|
| Request rate | How many requests per second |
| Response time | How fast requests are handled |
| Error rate | Percentage of failed requests |
| Cache hit rate | How often cached files are served |
| Database connections | Pool utilization |
| Redis memory | Cache memory usage |
| Disk usage | Cache directory size |

## 58.4 Health Checks

A simple health check endpoint:

```rust
.route("/health", get(|| async { "OK" }))
```

For more detailed health checks:

```rust
async fn health_check(State(state): State<Arc<AppState>>) -> Json<Value> {
    let db_ok = sqlx::query("SELECT 1").execute(&state.db).await.is_ok();
    let redis_ok = redis::cmd("PING").query_async(&mut state.redis.clone()).await.is_ok();

    Json(json!({
        "status": if db_ok && redis_ok { "healthy" } else { "degraded" },
        "database": db_ok,
        "redis": redis_ok,
    }))
}
```

# Chapter 59: Troubleshooting Common Issues

## 59.1 Database Connection Errors

**Problem**: `Failed to connect to database`

**Solutions**:
1. Check that PostgreSQL is running: `systemctl status postgresql`
2. Verify the connection string: `psql $DATABASE_URL`
3. Check firewall rules
4. Verify the database exists: `psql -c "\l"`

## 59.2 Redis Connection Errors

**Problem**: `Failed to connect to Redis`

**Solutions**:
1. Check that Redis is running: `redis-cli ping`
2. Verify the connection string
3. Check Redis logs: `journalctl -u redis`

## 59.3 Scraping Errors

**Problem**: `ScrapeError: fic not found`

**Solutions**:
1. Verify the URL is correct
2. Check if the source site is accessible
3. Look for rate limiting from the source site
4. Check the User-Agent header

## 59.4 EPUB Generation Errors

**Problem**: `ExportError: EPUB generation failed`

**Solutions**:
1. Check disk space in `TMP_DIR`
2. Verify file permissions
3. Check for invalid HTML in chapter content
4. Look at the error details in logs

## 59.5 Memory Issues

**Problem**: Server runs out of memory

**Solutions**:
1. Reduce `max_connections` in the database pool
2. Clean up old temporary files in `TMP_DIR`
3. Monitor cache directory size
4. Check for memory leaks in long-running tasks

## 59.6 Slow Requests

**Problem**: Requests take too long

**Solutions**:
1. Check database query performance with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`
2. Verify indexes are being used
3. Check network latency to source sites
4. Increase cache hit rate
5. Monitor concurrent request count

# Chapter 60: Glossary

## A

**Async/Await**: A programming pattern that allows code to perform long-running operations (like network requests) without blocking the main thread.

**Atom**: A syndication format (like RSS) used by OPDS feeds.

**Axum**: A Rust web framework built on top of Tower.

## B

**Backend**: The server-side part of a web application that processes requests, interacts with databases, and generates responses.

**Binary**: A compiled program that can be executed directly.

## C

**Cache**: A temporary storage layer that speeds up data access by storing frequently used data in a fast-access location.

**Crate**: A Rust package/library. Rust's equivalent of npm packages or pip packages.

**CORS**: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing — a security mechanism that controls which websites can make requests to your server.

## D

**Database**: An organized collection of structured data stored electronically.

**Docker**: A platform for building and running applications in isolated containers.

## E

**EPUB**: Electronic Publication — the standard format for e-books.

**Error Handling**: The process of detecting and responding to errors in code.

## F

**Fandom**: A community of fans of a particular work (e.g., "Harry Potter fandom").

**Full-Text Search**: A search technique that examines all words in a document.

## G

**GIN Index**: Generalized Inverted Index — a PostgreSQL index type optimized for full-text search.

## H

**HTML**: HyperText Markup Language — the standard language for web pages.

**HTTP**: HyperText Transfer Protocol — the protocol used for web communication.

## I

**IP Address**: Internet Protocol Address — a unique identifier for a device on a network.

## J

**Jaccard Similarity**: A statistic used for comparing the similarity of sample sets.

## K

**Kubernetes**: A container orchestration platform for managing scaled applications.

## L

**Lua**: A lightweight programming language used for scripting in Redis.

## M

**Middleware**: Software that sits between the raw HTTP request and the handler function.

**Migration**: A version-controlled script that modifies the database schema.

## O

**OPDS**: Open Publication Distribution System — a standard for e-book catalogs.

**Ownership**: Rust's memory management system that ensures data safety without a garbage collector.

## P

**PostgreSQL**: A powerful open-source relational database.

**Parameterized Query**: A SQL query where values are passed separately from the query string to prevent injection attacks.

## Q

**Query**: A request for data from a database.

## R

**Rate Limiting**: Controlling how fast users can make requests.

**Redis**: An in-memory data store used for caching and rate limiting.

**REST API**: An architectural style for web APIs using HTTP methods.

## S

**Scraper**: A program that automatically extracts data from websites.

**Semaphore**: A synchronization primitive that controls access to a shared resource.

**Serialization**: Converting data structures to a format that can be stored or transmitted.

**SQL**: Structured Query Language — the standard language for database operations.

**SQLx**: A Rust library for interacting with SQL databases.

## T

**Tag**: A keyword or label attached to a fanfiction story (e.g., "Fluff", "Harry Potter").

**Token Bucket**: A rate limiting algorithm that uses tokens to control request flow.

**Trait**: A Rust interface that defines methods that a type must implement.

## U

**Upsert**: A database operation that inserts a row if it does not exist, or updates it if it does.

## V

**Virtual DOM**: A programming concept where an efficient virtual representation of the UI is kept in memory.

## W

**WebSocket**: A communication protocol that provides full-duplex communication over a single TCP connection.

# Extended Chapter 1: The FicHub Story in Detail

## 1.A The Problem FicHub Solves

Let us imagine a scenario that happens every day. You are browsing Archive of Our Own, and you find a magnificent 200-chapter epic fanfiction. The story has incredible world-building, complex character development, and prose that would make professional authors jealous. You are completely hooked.

But there is a problem. You want to read this story on your commute to work, on the train where there is no internet connection. You could try to use your browser's built-in reader mode, but that only works online. You could try to copy-paste each chapter into a document, but with 200 chapters, that would take hours.

What you need is a way to download this story as an EPUB file — the same format that your Kindle or Kobo e-reader uses. You could search for a browser extension that does this, but those are often unreliable, ad-supported, or even malicious.

This is where FicHub comes in. FicHub is a web service that does this automatically. You give it a URL, and within seconds, you get back a beautifully formatted EPUB file with proper chapter navigation, metadata, and clean typography. It also generates HTML bundles for reading in a web browser, and can even convert to MOBI and PDF formats.

But FicHub is more than just a file converter. It is a complete fanfiction platform that includes:

- **Metadata Storage**: FicHub remembers every story it has ever processed, including word count, chapter count, publication dates, and author information.

- **Community Tagging**: Users can add tags to stories (like "Fluff", "Angst", "Slow Burn") and vote on whether tags are accurate. Tags that get too many downvotes are automatically hidden.

- **Advanced Search**: You can search for stories by title, author, tags, word count, completion status, and date range — all powered by PostgreSQL's full-text search engine.

- **Recommendation Engine**: FicHub suggests similar stories using collaborative filtering — the same technique Netflix and Spotify use. If two users like the same stories, FicHub can suggest that User A might enjoy stories that User B liked.

- **OPDS Catalog**: E-readers can connect directly to FicHub to browse and download stories, just like connecting to a library's digital catalog.

- **Background Collection Worker**: A background process continuously scrapes user favourites from fanfiction sites to build the data that powers recommendations.

## 1.B How FicHub Fits Into the Fanfiction Ecosystem

The fanfiction community is massive. Archive of Our Own alone hosts over 12 million works. FanFiction.net has been around since 1998 and has millions more. Sites like SpaceBattles, Sufficient Velocity, and various Harry Potter fanfiction sites add to the total.

These sites serve different purposes:
- **Archive of Our Own (AO3)**: The largest archive, known for its tag system and open policies
- **FanFiction.net (FF.net)**: One of the oldest sites, with a large catalog but stricter content policies
- **SpaceBattles/Sufficient Velocity**: Forum-based sites where stories are posted as threads
- **Various fandom-specific sites**: Like HPFF (Harry Potter Fan Fiction), Adult FanFiction, etc.

FicHub acts as a bridge between all of these sites. Instead of needing separate tools for each site, you just give FicHub any URL from any supported site, and it figures out the rest.

## 1.C The Architecture Philosophy

When designing FicHub's backend, the developers made several key decisions:

1. **Rust for performance**: Fanfiction stories can be very long (some are over a million words). Generating an EPUB for such a story requires processing a lot of HTML. Rust's speed ensures this happens quickly.

2. **PostgreSQL for reliability**: The fanfiction database grows continuously. PostgreSQL handles large datasets well and provides full-text search without needing a separate search engine.

3. **Redis for speed**: Rate limiting and caching need to be extremely fast. Redis handles these operations in sub-millisecond time.

4. **Modular design**: Each subsystem (scraping, exporting, tagging, recommendations) is independent and can be modified without affecting the others.

5. **Graceful degradation**: If one part of the system fails (e.g., Redis goes down), the rest continues to work. The server might not be able to rate-limit, but it can still serve requests.

## 1.D Real-World Usage Patterns

Based on the code, we can infer how FicHub is used:

- Most requests come through the EPUB export endpoint (`/api/v0/epub`)
- The metadata endpoint (`/api/v0/meta`) is used for previews
- OPDS feeds are used by e-reader apps for browsing
- The search endpoint powers the frontend's search functionality
- Tags and recommendations are used by power users who want to discover new stories
- The curator system is used by a small team of trusted moderators

## 1.E Performance Characteristics

Let us think about what makes FicHub fast:

- **Scraping**: Each story requires 1-N HTTP requests (depending on chapter count). AO3 supports a `?view_full_work=true` parameter that returns all chapters on one page, making single requests possible.

- **EPUB generation**: The `epub-builder` crate is pure Rust and very fast. Even for a 200-chapter story, EPUB generation takes less than a second.

- **Caching**: Once generated, EPUBs are served directly from disk. The disk cache can handle thousands of concurrent reads.

- **Database queries**: PostgreSQL with proper indexes handles most queries in under a millisecond.

- **Rate limiting**: The Redis-backed token bucket adds minimal overhead (sub-millisecond per request).

# Extended Chapter 2: Technology Deep Dive

## 2.A Rust's Ownership System

Rust's most unique feature is its ownership system. In most programming languages, you can have multiple variables pointing to the same data. In Rust, each piece of data has exactly one owner.

```rust
fn main() {
    let s1 = String::from("hello");
    let s2 = s1;  // s1 is "moved" to s2
    // println!("{}", s1);  // ERROR: s1 is no longer valid!
    println!("{}", s2);     // This works
}
```

When `s1` is assigned to `s2`, the ownership transfers. `s1` is no longer valid. This prevents common bugs like double-free errors.

For shared access, Rust provides borrowing:

```rust
fn main() {
    let s1 = String::from("hello");
    let len = calculate_length(&s1);  // Borrow s1
    println!("Length of '{}' is {}.", s1, len);  // s1 is still valid!
}

fn calculate_length(s: &String) -> usize {
    s.len()
}  // s goes out of scope, but since it does not own the data, nothing is dropped
```

The `&` creates a reference (borrow) without taking ownership.

## 2.B Understanding Traits in Depth

Traits are one of Rust's most powerful features. They define shared behavior:

```rust
// Define a trait
trait Summary {
    fn summarize(&self) -> String;

    // Default implementation
    fn preview(&self) -> String {
        format!("{}...", &self.summarize()[..50])
    }
}

// Implement the trait for a type
struct Article {
    title: String,
    author: String,
    content: String,
}

impl Summary for Article {
    fn summarize(&self) -> String {
        format!("{}, by {} - {}", self.title, self.author, &self.content[..100])
    }
}

// Use the trait
fn notify(item: &impl Summary) {
    println!("Breaking news! {}", item.summarize());
}
```

FicHub uses traits extensively:

- `SiteScraper`: Defines how to scrape different websites
- `RateLimiter`: Defines how to limit request rates
- `SiteFetcher`: Defines how to collect user favourites

## 2.C Enums and Pattern Matching

Rust's enums are more powerful than enums in other languages. They can hold data:

```rust
enum AppError {
    BadRequest(i32, String),
    RateLimited(u64),
    NotFound(String),
    Internal(String),
    ScrapeError(String),
    ExportError(String),
    Database(String),
    CacheError(String),
}

fn handle_error(err: AppError) {
    match err {
        AppError::BadRequest(code, msg) => {
            println!("Bad request {}: {}", code, msg);
        }
        AppError::RateLimited(seconds) => {
            println!("Rate limited, retry in {}s", seconds);
        }
        AppError::NotFound(msg) => {
            println!("Not found: {}", msg);
        }
        _ => {
            println!("Internal error");
        }
    }
}
```

The `match` expression must handle every possible variant, which prevents forgotten error cases.

## 2.D Error Handling with the ? Operator

The `?` operator is syntactic sugar for error propagation:

```rust
// Without ?
fn read_config() -> Result<Config, AppError> {
    let content = match std::fs::read_to_string("config.toml") {
        Ok(c) => c,
        Err(e) => return Err(AppError::Internal(e.to_string())),
    };
    let config = match toml::from_str(&content) {
        Ok(c) => c,
        Err(e) => return Err(AppError::Internal(e.to_string())),
    };
    Ok(config)
}

// With ?
fn read_config() -> Result<Config, AppError> {
    let content = std::fs::read_to_string("config.toml")?;  // Auto-converts io::Error
    let config = toml::from_str(&content)?;  // Auto-converts toml::Error
    Ok(config)
}
```

FicHub's `From` implementations enable this:

```rust
impl From<std::io::Error> for AppError {
    fn from(err: std::io::Error) -> Self {
        AppError::Internal(err.to_string())
    }
}

impl From<sqlx::Error> for AppError {
    fn from(err: sqlx::Error) -> Self {
        AppError::Database(err.to_string())
    }
}
```

## 2.E Concurrency in Rust

Rust's type system prevents data races at compile time. Here are the key concepts:

### Threads

```rust
use std::thread;

let handle = thread::spawn(|| {
    println!("Hello from a thread!");
});

handle.join().unwrap();  // Wait for the thread to finish
```

### Channels

```rust
use std::sync::mpsc;

let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel();

thread::spawn(move || {
    let data = String::from("hello");
    tx.send(data).unwrap();
});

let received = rx.recv().unwrap();
```

### Mutex

```rust
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};

let counter = Arc::new(Mutex::new(0));
let mut handles = vec![];

for _ in 0..10 {
    let counter = Arc::clone(&counter);
    let handle = thread::spawn(move || {
        let mut num = counter.lock().unwrap();
        *num += 1;
    });
    handles.push(handle);
}

for handle in handles {
    handle.join().unwrap();
}
```

### Arc (Atomic Reference Counting)

`Arc` allows multiple threads to share ownership of data:

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;

let data = Arc::new(vec![1, 2, 3]);

for _ in 0..3 {
    let data = Arc::clone(&data);
    thread::spawn(move || {
        println!("{:?}", data);
    });
}
```

FicHub uses `Arc` extensively for sharing `AppState` across async tasks.

### Feature Flags

Notice the `features` array on some dependencies. Feature flags enable optional functionality:

```toml
sqlx = { version = "0.8", features = ["runtime-tokio", "postgres"] }
```

This enables:
- `runtime-tokio`: Integration with the Tokio async runtime
- `postgres`: PostgreSQL database support

Without these features, SQLx would not know how to connect to PostgreSQL or run async queries.

## 3.C Understanding the Target Directory

When you run `cargo build`, Cargo creates a `target/` directory:

```
target/
├── debug/              # Debug build (fast to compile, slow to run)
│   ├── fichub          # The executable
│   └── deps/           # Compiled dependencies
├── release/            # Release build (slow to compile, fast to run)
│   ├── fichub
│   └── deps/
└── debug/.fingerprint/ # Build cache (speeds up incremental builds)
```

- **Debug builds** are faster to compile but run slower because they include debug information and do not optimize the code.
- **Release builds** take longer to compile but run much faster because the compiler optimizes the code.

For development, use `cargo run` (debug). For deployment, use `cargo build --release`.

## 4.B Visibility Rules

In Rust, items are private by default. The `pub` keyword makes them public:

```rust
// Private (only visible within this module)
fn internal_helper() -> String { "secret".to_string() }

// Public (visible from outside this module)
pub fn public_api() -> String { internal_helper() }
```

Modules can also have visibility:

```rust
pub mod routes;      // Public module
mod internal;        // Private module
pub(crate) mod utils; // Public within this crate only
```

## 4.C Re-exports

The `pub use` statement re-exports items from sub-modules:

```rust
// In lib.rs
pub use routes::export::{build_info_string, build_meta_json, generate_slug};
pub use scrape::ExtractedTag;
```

This means other code can access these items as:
```rust
use fichub::generate_slug;  // Instead of fichub::routes::export::generate_slug
```

## 4.D Circular Dependencies

Rust prevents circular dependencies between modules. If module A depends on module B, module B cannot depend on module A. This forces a clean dependency hierarchy.

In FicHub, the dependency flow is:
1. `main` depends on `server` and `config`
2. `server` depends on `db`, `cache`, `scrape`, `routes`, `recommender`, `limiter`
3. `routes` depends on `db`, `scrape`, `cache`, `export`, `tags`, `search`, `recommender`
4. Lower-level modules (`db`, `cache`, `scrape`) have minimal dependencies

# Extended Chapter 5: First Code Walkthrough

## 5.A Reading main.rs Line by Line

Let us read every single line of `main.rs` and understand exactly what it does:

```rust
// Line 1-13: Module declarations
pub mod cache;      // Makes the cache module public
pub mod config;     // Makes the config module public
pub mod db;         // Makes the database module public
pub mod error;      // Makes the error module public
pub mod export;     // Makes the export module public
pub mod frontend;   // Makes the frontend module public
pub mod limiter;    // Makes the rate limiter module public
pub mod recommender;// Makes the recommender module public
pub mod routes;     // Makes the routes module public
pub mod scrape;     // Makes the scrape module public
pub mod search;     // Makes the search module public
pub mod server;     // Makes the server module public
pub mod tags;       // Makes the tags module public

// Line 15: The #[tokio::main] attribute
// This transforms our main function to use the Tokio async runtime.
// Without this, we could not use .await or async functions.
#[tokio::main]

// Line 16: async fn main()
// The async keyword means this function is asynchronous.
// It can perform non-blocking I/O operations.
async fn main() {
    // Line 18: Load .env file
    // dotenvy::dotenv() reads a .env file and sets environment variables
    // .ok() means "if it fails, that is fine" (no .env file is OK)
    dotenvy::dotenv().ok();

    // Line 21-26: Initialize tracing (logging system)
    // tracing_subscriber::fmt() creates a formatter for log messages
    // .with_env_filter() controls which messages are shown based on RUST_LOG
    // .init() starts the logging system
    tracing_subscriber::fmt()
        .with_env_filter(
            tracing_subscriber::EnvFilter::try_from_default_env()
                .unwrap_or_else(|_| tracing_subscriber::EnvFilter::new("info,fichub=debug")),
        )
        .init();

    // Line 28-29: Load configuration
    // Config::from_env() reads all environment variables and creates a Config struct
    let config = config::Config::from_env();

    // Line 31-32: Log the startup message
    // tracing::info! macro creates a log message at the INFO level
    tracing::info!("Starting fichub-rs server on port {}", config.app_port);

    // Line 34-35: Start the server
    // server::run(config) sets up and starts the web server
    // .await waits for the server to start (it runs forever)
    server::run(config).await;
}
```

# Extended Chapter 6: Configuration Deep Dive

## 6.A The Config Loading Process

Let us trace exactly how the configuration is loaded:

```rust
pub fn from_env() -> Self {
    // Step 1: Read DATABASE_URL (required)
    // If this is not set, the program crashes with a clear message
    let database_url = std::env::var("DATABASE_URL")
        .expect("DATABASE_URL must be set");

    // Step 2: Read REDIS_URL (required)
    let redis_url = std::env::var("REDIS_URL")
        .expect("REDIS_URL must be set");

    // Step 3: Read CACHE_DIR (optional, default: "./cache")
    // .unwrap_or_else() provides a default if the variable is not set
    let cache_dir = std::env::var("CACHE_DIR")
        .unwrap_or_else(|_| "./cache".to_string());

    // Step 4: Read SECONDARY_CACHE_DIR (optional, can be empty)
    // .ok() converts Result to Option
    // .filter() removes empty strings
    // .map() converts String to PathBuf
    let secondary_cache_dir = std::env::var("SECONDARY_CACHE_DIR")
        .ok()
        .filter(|s| !s.is_empty())
        .map(PathBuf::from);

    // Step 5: Read EXPORT_VERSION (optional, default: 1)
    // .parse().unwrap_or(1) handles invalid values gracefully
    let export_version = std::env::var("EXPORT_VERSION")
        .unwrap_or_else(|_| "1".to_string())
        .parse()
        .unwrap_or(1);

    // Step 6: Read DYNAMIC_RATE_LIMIT (optional, default: true)
    // .parse::<bool>() handles "true"/"false" strings
    let dynamic_rate_limit = std::env::var("DYNAMIC_RATE_LIMIT")
        .unwrap_or_else(|_| "true".to_string())
        .parse::<bool>()
        .unwrap_or(true);

    // ... (more settings follow the same pattern)

    // Step N: Construct and return the Config struct
    Config {
        database_url,
        redis_url,
        cache_dir: PathBuf::from(cache_dir),
        secondary_cache_dir,
        export_version,
        dynamic_rate_limit,
        // ...
    }
}
```

## 6.B Understanding the Parsing Chain

Let us trace the parsing chain for a numeric setting:

```rust
let app_port = std::env::var("PORT")                    // Result<String, VarError>
    .unwrap_or_else(|_| "3000".to_string())              // String
    .parse()                                              // Result<u16, ParseIntError>
    .unwrap_or(3000);                                     // u16
```

Each step:
1. `std::env::var("PORT")` — Returns `Ok("8080")` or `Err(VarError::NotPresent)`
2. `.unwrap_or_else(|_| "3000".to_string())` — If Err, use "3000" as default
3. `.parse()` — Tries to parse the string as a `u16`. Returns `Ok(8080)` or `Err(ParseIntError)`
4. `.unwrap_or(3000)` — If parsing failed, use 3000 as default

This chain handles three possible failure modes:
- Variable not set → uses default "3000"
- Variable set to non-numeric → uses default 3000
- Variable set to valid number → uses that number

## 6.C The EnvGuard Pattern in Detail

The test infrastructure for configuration is sophisticated:

```rust
struct EnvGuard {
    keys: Vec<String>,
}

impl EnvGuard {
    fn new() -> Self {
        EnvGuard { keys: Vec::new() }
    }

    fn set(&mut self, key: &str, val: &str) {
        self.keys.push(key.to_string());
        unsafe { std::env::set_var(key, val); }
    }
}

impl Drop for EnvGuard {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        for key in &self.keys {
            unsafe { std::env::remove_var(key); }
        }
    }
}
```

This is a "guard" pattern. When the `EnvGuard` is created, it starts tracking which environment variables have been set. When it is dropped (goes out of scope), it automatically cleans up by removing those variables.

The `unsafe` keyword is needed because `std::env::set_var` and `std::env::remove_var` are unsafe functions — they modify global state that is shared across threads. The `ENV_LOCK` mutex ensures only one test at a time modifies environment variables.

# Extended Chapter 7: The Axum Framework

## 7.A Understanding Axum's Architecture

Axum is built on three core concepts:

1. **Extractors**: Automatically parse request data into Rust types
2. **Handlers**: Functions that process requests and return responses
3. **Middleware**: Layers that wrap handlers to add behavior

### Extractors

Extractors automatically extract data from requests:

```rust
// State extractor - gets shared application state
async fn handler(State(state): State<Arc<AppState>>) { }

// Query extractor - gets URL query parameters
async fn handler(Query(params): Query<MyParams>) { }

// Path extractor - gets URL path parameters
async fn handler(Path(id): Path<i32>) { }

// Json extractor - gets JSON request body
async fn handler(Json(body): Json<MyBody>) { }

// ConnectInfo extractor - gets client IP address
async fn handler(ConnectInfo(addr): ConnectInfo<SocketAddr>) { }
```

### Handlers

Handlers are async functions that return a response:

```rust
// Return JSON
async fn handler() -> Json<Value> {
    Json(json!({"status": "ok"}))
}

// Return with status code
async fn handler() -> (StatusCode, Json<Value>) {
    (StatusCode::CREATED, Json(json!({"id": 1})))
}

// Return custom response
async fn handler() -> impl IntoResponse {
    ([("X-Custom", "value")], "Hello").into_response()
}
```

### Middleware

Middleware wraps handlers to add behavior:

```rust
let app = Router::new()
    .route("/", get(handler))
    .layer(TraceLayer::new_for_http())  // Add logging
    .layer(CorsLayer::permissive());     // Add CORS headers
```

## 7.B The Request Lifecycle

Here is what happens when a request arrives at the server:

```
1. TCP connection accepted by TcpListener
2. HTTP request parsed by hyper (low-level HTTP library)
3. Request enters the Axum middleware stack:
   a. TraceLayer logs the request
   b. CorsLayer adds CORS headers
4. Router matches the URL to a handler function
5. Extractors parse the request:
   a. State extracts the shared AppState
   b. Query parses URL parameters
   c. ConnectInfo extracts the client IP
6. Handler function is called with extracted data
7. Handler returns a response
8. Response passes back through middleware
9. Response is sent to the client
```

## 7.C Type Safety in Routes

One of Axum's best features is type safety. If you define a query parameter struct:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Deserialize)]
pub struct ExportQuery {
    pub q: Option<String>,
    pub automated: Option<String>,
}
```

Axum automatically:
- Parses the URL query string
- Deserializes it into the struct
- Returns a 400 error if parsing fails
- Passes the struct to your handler

You never need to manually parse query strings!

## 7.D State Sharing Patterns

FicHub uses `Arc<AppState>` for sharing state:

```rust
let state = Arc::new(AppState { /* ... */ });

let app = Router::new()
    .route("/api/v0/epub", get(epub_handler))
    .with_state(state);
```

Each handler receives the state:

```rust
async fn epub_handler(
    State(state): State<Arc<AppState>>,
) -> Result<Json<Value>, AppError> {
    // state.db — database pool
    // state.config — configuration
    // state.http_client — HTTP client for scraping
    // state.scraper_registry — all scrapers
    // etc.
}
```

# Extended Chapter 8: The Database Layer

## 8.A SQLx Features

SQLx provides several key features that FicHub uses:

### Compile-Time Checked Queries

```rust
// This query is checked against the actual database at compile time
let story = sqlx::query_as::<_, FicInfo>(
    "SELECT * FROM fic_info WHERE id = $1"
)
.bind("abc123")
.fetch_one(&pool)
.await?;
```

If the table name is wrong, or a column does not exist, you get a compile error.

### Type-Safe Parameters

```rust
// SQLx knows $1 should be a String because we .bind a String
sqlx::query("SELECT * FROM fic_info WHERE id = $1")
    .bind(some_string)  // Type-checked!
    .fetch_one(&pool)
    .await?;
```

### Automatic Connection Pooling

```rust
let pool = PgPoolOptions::new()
    .max_connections(20)
    .connect(database_url)
    .await?;
```

SQLx handles borrowing connections from the pool and returning them automatically.

## 8.B Working with Migrations

### Running Migrations

```rust
let migrations_path = Path::new("migrations");
sqlx::migrate::Migrator::new(migrations_path)
    .await?
    .run(&pool)
    .await?;
```

### Creating Migrations

Use the SQLx CLI:
```bash
cargo install sqlx-cli
sqlx migrate add add_tags_table
```

This creates a timestamped SQL file in the `migrations/` directory.

### Migration Safety

Migrations should be:
1. **Idempotent**: Running them twice should not cause errors
2. **Backward compatible**: Old code should still work after the migration
3. **Tested**: Always test on a copy of production data first

## 8.C Query Performance

### EXPLAIN ANALYZE

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT fi.*, ts_rank(fi.text_search, plainto_tsquery('english', 'harry potter')) AS rank
FROM fic_info fi
WHERE fi.text_search @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'harry potter')
ORDER BY rank DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

This shows:
- The query plan (sequential scan vs. index scan)
- Estimated vs. actual row counts
- Execution time

### Index Strategy

For FicHub's workload, these indexes are important:

```sql
-- Primary key (auto-created)
-- fic_info(id) — used for most lookups

-- Full-text search
CREATE INDEX idx_fic_info_text_search ON fic_info USING gin(text_search);

-- Tag queries
CREATE INDEX idx_fic_tags_url_id ON fic_tags(url_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_fic_tags_tag_id ON fic_tags(tag_id);

-- Recommendation queries
CREATE INDEX idx_fic_bookmarks_url_id ON fic_bookmarks(url_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_fic_bookmarks_user_hash ON fic_bookmarks(user_hash);
```

## 8.D Connection Pool Monitoring

In production, you should monitor the connection pool:

```rust
// Get pool statistics
let stats = pool.options().get_max_connections();
tracing::info!("Max connections: {}", stats);

// Check for idle connections
// (This would be done through PostgreSQL's pg_stat_activity view)
```

# Extended Chapter 9: Error Handling Patterns

## 9.A The Error Hierarchy

FicHub's error types form a hierarchy:

```
AppError (public, returned to handlers)
├── BadRequest(400) — invalid input
├── RateLimited(429) — too many requests
├── NotFound(404) — resource not found
├── Internal(500) — unexpected errors
├── ScrapeError(502) — external service failure
├── ExportError(500) — file generation failure
├── Database(500) — database errors
└── CacheError(500) — cache errors
```

## 9.B Error Conversion Chain

When an error occurs, it flows through this chain:

```
External error (io::Error, sqlx::Error, etc.)
    ↓ (From impl)
AppError
    ↓ (IntoResponse impl)
HTTP Response
    ↓
Client receives JSON error response
```

## 9.C The ? Operator in Practice

Let us trace a complex function:

```rust
pub async fn epub_handler(
    State(state): State<Arc<AppState>>,
    Query(params): Query<ExportQuery>,
) -> Result<Json<Value>, AppError> {
    // Step 1: Parse query (can fail → BadRequest)
    let query = params.q.as_deref().unwrap_or("");
    if query.is_empty() {
        return Ok(Json(json!({"err": -1, "msg": "no query"})));
    }

    // Step 2: Find scraper (can fail → BadRequest)
    let scraper = state.scraper_registry.find_scraper(query)
        .ok_or_else(|| AppError::BadRequest(-5, format!("unsupported URL")))?

    // Step 3: Lookup metadata (can fail → ScrapeError)
    let meta = scraper.lookup(&state.http_client, query).await
        .map_err(|e| AppError::ScrapeError(e.to_string()))?;

    // Step 4: Database upsert (can fail → Database)
    queries::upsert_fic_info(&state.db, &fic_info_row).await?;

    // Step 5: Check blacklists (can fail → Database)
    let fic_blacklist = queries::check_fic_blacklist(&state.db, &meta.url_id).await?;

    // ... more steps

    // Step N: Return success
    Ok(Json(json!({"err": 0, "url_id": meta.url_id})))
}
```

Each `?` propagates errors up the stack, converting them to `AppError` along the way.

## 9.D Logging Errors

FicHub logs errors at different levels:

```rust
// Internal errors are logged at ERROR level
AppError::Internal(msg) => {
    tracing::error!("Internal error: {}", msg);
    (StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, json!({"err": -1, "msg": "internal error"}))
}

// Database errors are logged at ERROR level
AppError::Database(msg) => {
    tracing::error!("Database error: {}", msg);
    (StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, json!({"err": -1, "msg": "database error"}))
}

// Scrape errors are NOT logged (they are expected)
AppError::ScrapeError(msg) => {
    (StatusCode::BAD_GATEWAY, json!({"err": -6, "msg": msg}))
}
```

This distinction is important — internal errors indicate bugs that need fixing, while scrape errors are expected when source sites are unavailable.

# Extended Chapter 10: The Scraper System

## 10.A How HTML Parsing Works

When FicHub scrapes a website, it follows these steps:

### Step 1: Download the HTML

```rust
let response = client
    .get(&url)
    .header("User-Agent", "fichub.net/0.1.0")
    .send()
    .await?;

let html = response.text().await?;
```

### Step 2: Parse into a Document Tree

```rust
let document = Html::parse_document(&html);
```

This creates a tree structure from the HTML:

```
<html>
├── <head>
│   └── <title>My Story</title>
└── <body>
    ├── <h1 class="title">My Story</h1>
    ├── <p class="author">by Jane</p>
    └── <div class="content">
        └── <p>Once upon a time...</p>
    </div>
</body>
```

### Step 3: Find Elements with CSS Selectors

```rust
let selector = Selector::parse("h1.title").unwrap();
let title_element = document.select(&selector).next();
```

The CSS selector `h1.title` means "find an `<h1>` element with class `title`".

### Step 4: Extract Data

```rust
let title = title_element
    .map(|el| el.text().collect::<String>().trim().to_string())
    .unwrap_or_default();
```

`text()` returns an iterator over all text nodes inside the element. `collect::<String>()` joins them into a single string.

## 10.B Common CSS Selectors

| Selector | What It Matches | Example |
|----------|----------------|---------|
| `h1` | `<h1>` elements | Story title |
| `.title` | Elements with class "title" | Any element |
| `#story` | Element with id "story" | Specific element |
| `div.content` | `<div>` with class "content" | Story content |
| `a[rel='author']` | `<a>` with rel="author" | Author link |
| `dd.words` | `<dd>` with class "words" | Word count |
| `div.chapter h3` | `<h3>` inside a div with class "chapter" | Chapter title |
| `select#chap_select option[selected]` | Selected option in chapter dropdown | Chapter name |

## 10.C Handling Different Page Structures

Each website has a different HTML structure. The scrapers handle these differences:

### AO3 Structure

```html
<div id="workskin">
  <h2 class="title heading">My Story</h2>
  <h3 class="byline heading">
    <a href="/users/author" rel="author">Author Name</a>
  </h3>
  <div class="chapter">
    <h3 class="heading">Chapter 1</h3>
    <div class="userstuff">
      <p>Chapter content here...</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
```

Selector: `h2.title.heading` for title, `a[rel='author']` for author, `div.chapter` for chapters.

### FF.net Structure

```html
<div id="profile_top">
  <b class="xcontrast_txt">Story Title</b>
  <a class="xcontrast_txt" href="/u/12345">Author Name</a>
  <span class="xgray">Chapters: 10/10 - Words: 50,000</span>
</div>
<div class="storytext" id="storytext">
  <p>Chapter content here...</p>
</div>
```

Selector: `#profile_top b.xcontrast_txt` for title, `#profile_top a.xcontrast_txt` for author.

## 10.D The Extract Tags Feature

Some sites expose structured tags that FicHub can extract:

### AO3 Tags

AO3 has a rich tagging system. FicHub can extract:
- Fandom tags (e.g., "Harry Potter - J.K. Rowling")
- Character tags (e.g., "Harry Potter", "Hermione Granger")
- Relationship tags (e.g., "Harry Potter/Hermione Granger")
- Freeform tags (e.g., "Fluff", "Angst", "Slow Burn")
- Warning tags (e.g., "Major Character Death")

### FF.net Categories

FF.net has:
- Category (e.g., "Harry Potter")
- Genre (e.g., "Romance", "Adventure")
- Rating (e.g., "T")

These are extracted and stored as tags in the database.

## 10.E Rate Limiting for Scrapers

FicHub respects the rate limits of source sites:

```rust
// AO3: 1 request per 2 seconds
// FF.net: 1 request per 5 seconds
// XenForo: 1 request per 3 seconds
```

The `PerSiteRateLimiter` in the collection worker enforces these limits:

```rust
pub struct PerSiteRateLimiter {
    last_request: AtomicI64,  // Timestamp of last request
    delay_secs: u64,          // Minimum delay between requests
}
```

## 10.F Error Handling in Scrapers

Scrapers handle various error conditions:

```rust
pub enum ScrapeError {
    NotFound,           // Story does not exist
    Blocked,            // Site is blocking our requests
    Network(String),    // Network error
    ParseError(String), // Could not parse the page
}
```

Each scraper maps HTTP errors to appropriate `ScrapeError` variants:

```rust
if !response.status().is_success() {
    return Err(ScrapeError::NotFound);
}
```

# Extended Chapter 11: The Export Engine

## 11.A EPUB Format Internals

An EPUB file is actually a ZIP file containing:

```
mimetype                    # Must be first, uncompressed
META-INF/
  container.xml            # Points to the OPF file
OEBPS/
  content.opf              # Package document (metadata + manifest)
  toc.ncx                  # Table of contents (for older readers)
  toc.xhtml                # Table of contents (for newer readers)
  stylesheet.css           # Stylesheet
  introduction.xhtml       # First page (metadata)
  chapter_1.xhtml          # Chapter content
  chapter_2.xhtml
  ...
```

The `epub-builder` crate handles all of this automatically.

## 11.B HTML Cleaning

Before inserting story content into EPUB, FicHub cleans the HTML:

```rust
fn escape_html(s: &str) -> String {
    s.replace('&', "&amp;")
        .replace('<', "&lt;")
        .replace('>', "&gt;")
        .replace('"', "&quot;")
        .replace('\'', "&#39;")
}
```

This is important because:
1. The source HTML might contain scripts or other dangerous content
2. Special characters in EPUB XML could break the format
3. User-generated content should never be trusted

## 11.C The Conversion Pipeline

When a user requests MOBI or PDF, the pipeline is:

```
Scrape story → Generate EPUB → Convert via Calibre → Serve converted file
```

The Calibre conversion happens in a subprocess:

```rust
Command::new("ebook-convert")
    .arg(epub_path)
    .arg(output_path)
    .output()
    .await
```

With a 300-second timeout:

```rust
timeout(Duration::from_secs(300), async {
    Command::new("ebook-convert")
        .arg(epub_path)
        .arg(output_path)
        .output()
        .await
}).await
```

If the conversion hangs, it is killed after 5 minutes.

## 11.D Cache Invalidation

When a story is updated on the source site, cached exports become stale. FicHub handles this through:

1. **Content hash**: Each export includes a hash of the source content
2. **Version bumps**: The `fic_version_bump` table tracks updates
3. **Cache lookup**: When serving a cached file, FicHub checks if the hash matches

```rust
let version_bump = queries::get_fic_version_bump(&state.db, &meta.url_id)
    .await?.unwrap_or(0);
let version = state.config.export_version + version_bump;
```

# Extended Chapter 12: Rate Limiting

## 12.A The Token Bucket Algorithm

Let us walk through a complete example of the token bucket:

```
Configuration:
  Capacity: 10 tokens
  Flow rate: 2 tokens per second
  Request cost: 1 token

Time 0.0s:
  Bucket: 10/10 tokens
  Request arrives → consume 1 token
  Bucket: 9/10 tokens → Allowed ✓

Time 0.1s:
  Bucket: 9/10 tokens (no refill yet, only 0.2s elapsed)
  Request arrives → consume 1 token
  Bucket: 8/10 tokens → Allowed ✓

Time 0.5s:
  Bucket: 8 + 1 = 9/10 tokens (refilled 2 * 0.5 = 1 token)
  Request arrives → consume 1 token
  Bucket: 8/10 tokens → Allowed ✓

Time 1.0s:
  Bucket: 8 + 1 = 9/10 tokens (refilled 2 * 0.5 = 1 token)
  Rapid fire: 10 requests
  First 9 requests → consume 9 tokens → Bucket: 0/10
  10th request → needs 1 token, only 0 available
  Wait time: (1 - 0) / 2 = 0.5 seconds → Wait ⏳
```

## 12.B The Lua Script

The Lua script runs atomically in Redis:

```lua
-- Read current state
local bucket = redis.call('HMGET', key, 'value', 'last_drain')
local value = tonumber(bucket[1])
local last_drain = tonumber(bucket[2])

-- Get current time (Redis server time)
local now = redis.call('TIME')
local now_sec = tonumber(now[1]) + tonumber(now[2])/1000000

-- Initialize if first request
if value == nil then
    value = capacity
    last_drain = now_sec
    redis.call('HMSET', key, 'value', value, 'last_drain', last_drain)
end

-- Calculate tokens available
local elapsed = now_sec - last_drain
local new_tokens = math.min(capacity, value + elapsed * flow)
local allowed = new_tokens - requested

if allowed >= 0 then
    -- Enough tokens: deduct and update
    redis.call('HMSET', key, 'value', allowed, 'last_drain', now_sec)
    return -1  -- -1 means "allowed"
else
    -- Not enough tokens: calculate wait time
    local wait = (requested - new_tokens) / flow
    return wait  -- Positive number = seconds to wait
end
```

This runs as a single atomic operation in Redis, so concurrent requests are handled correctly.

## 12.C Two-Tier Rate Limiting

FicHub's two-tier system:

```
Request arrives
    ↓
┌──────────────────┐
│ Global Bucket     │
│ Capacity: 150    │
│ Flow: 30/sec     │
│                   │
│ Allows: 30 req/s │
│ across ALL users  │
└────────┬─────────┘
         ↓ (if allowed)
┌──────────────────┐
│ Per-IP Bucket     │
│ Capacity: 30     │
│ Flow: ~0.12/sec  │
│                   │
│ Allows: ~1 req   │
│ per 8.6 seconds  │
│ per IP address    │
└────────┬─────────┘
         ↓ (if allowed)
   Request processed
```

The global bucket prevents the server from being overwhelmed, while the per-IP bucket prevents individual users from consuming all the resources.

## 12.D Static vs. Dynamic Rate Limiting

FicHub supports two modes:

### Dynamic Mode (default)

Uses the token bucket algorithm with Redis. Provides smooth, adaptive rate limiting.

### Static Mode

Uses a simple random delay:

```rust
if !self.dynamic_rate_limit {
    let delay = self.static_delay_base + rand::random::<f64>() * self.static_delay_base;
    tokio::time::sleep(tokio::time::Duration::from_secs_f64(delay)).await;
    return RateLimitResult::Allowed;
}
```

Static mode adds a random delay between 0.1 and 0.2 seconds to each request. This is simpler but less efficient.

# Extended Chapter 13: The Tagging System

## 13.A Tag Resolution Flow

When a user submits a tag, here is the complete flow:

```
User submits tag "fluff"
    ↓
Step 1: Check tags table
  SELECT id, name, tag_type_id FROM tags WHERE name = 'fluff'
  → Found? Return existing tag
  → Not found? Continue ↓

Step 2: Check tag_aliases table
  SELECT canonical_tag_id FROM tag_aliases WHERE alias_name = 'fluff'
  → Found? Look up the canonical tag and return it
  → Not found? Continue ↓

Step 3: Create new tag
  INSERT INTO tags (name, tag_type_id) VALUES ('fluff', 4) RETURNING id
  → Return new tag with is_new = true
```

## 13.B The Voting System

The voting system uses a PostgreSQL trigger to automatically update scores:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION update_fic_tag_score() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
    -- Recalculate the aggregate score from all votes
    UPDATE fic_tags SET score = (
        SELECT COALESCE(SUM(value), 0)
        FROM fic_tag_votes
        WHERE url_id = NEW.url_id AND tag_id = NEW.tag_id
    )
    WHERE url_id = NEW.url_id AND tag_id = NEW.tag_id;
    RETURN NEW;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER update_fic_tag_score_trigger
    AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE ON fic_tag_votes
    FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION update_fic_tag_score();
```

This means:
1. A vote is inserted/updated in `fic_tag_votes`
2. The trigger fires automatically
3. The trigger recalculates the score by summing all votes
4. The score is updated in `fic_tags`

The application code does not need to manually recalculate scores!

## 13.C Auto-Moderation

When a tag's score drops below the threshold, it is automatically hidden:

```rust
pub fn is_hidden(score: i16, threshold: i16) -> bool {
    score <= threshold
}
```

The default threshold is -3. So if a tag has 1 upvote and 4 downvotes (score = -3), it becomes hidden.

Optionally, tags can be auto-deleted:

```rust
pub tag_auto_delete_threshold: Option<i16>,
```

If this is set (e.g., to -10), tags with scores at or below this threshold are automatically removed from the database.

## 13.D The Curator System

Curators are trusted users who can:

1. **Create aliases**: Map alternative names to canonical tags
   - "hp" → "Harry Potter"
   - "hermione" → "Hermione Granger"

2. **Merge tags**: Combine duplicate tags
   - Merge "Hermione Granger" into "Hermione Jean Granger"

3. **Delete tags**: Remove inappropriate or unused tags
   - Delete tags with no fic associations

4. **Resolve flags**: Address user-submitted reports
   - Review flagged tags and mark as resolved

# Extended Chapter 14: The Recommendation Engine

## 14.A Collaborative Filtering in Detail

The recommendation engine uses user-user collaborative filtering:

### Step 1: Identify Similar Users

For a given story, find users who also favourited it:

```sql
SELECT user_hash FROM fic_bookmarks WHERE url_id = $1
```

### Step 2: Find Their Other Favourites

For each similar user, find what else they favourited:

```sql
SELECT url_id FROM fic_bookmarks WHERE user_hash = $2 AND url_id != $1
```

### Step 3: Count Co-occurrences

Count how many users favourited both the seed story and each candidate:

```sql
SELECT
    CASE WHEN work_a = $1 THEN work_b ELSE work_a END AS candidate_id,
    cooccur_count
FROM fic_bookmark_cooccur
WHERE work_a = $1 OR work_b = $1
```

### Step 4: Calculate Jaccard Similarity

```rust
let jaccard = cooccur_count as f64 / (seed_count + candidate_count - cooccur_count);
```

### Step 5: Blend with Tag-Based Scores

```rust
let weight = (favouriter_count as f64 / 5.0).min(1.0);
let final_score = collab_score * weight + tag_score * (1.0 - weight);
```

### Step 6: Apply Community Boost

```rust
let boost = 1.0 + gamma * (net_votes.max(0) as f64).ln_1p();
final_score *= boost;
```

## 14.B The Collection Worker

The collection worker runs in the background and:

1. Polls Redis queues for new work items
2. Scrapes user favourites from fanfiction sites
3. Builds co-occurrence data
4. Updates the `fic_works` table with favouriter counts

### Rate Limiting

Each site has its own rate limiter:

```rust
pub struct PerSiteRateLimiter {
    last_request: AtomicI64,
    delay_secs: u64,
}

impl PerSiteRateLimiter {
    pub async fn wait_if_needed(&self) {
        loop {
            let now = SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).unwrap().as_nanos() as i64;
            let last = self.last_request.load(Ordering::Acquire);
            let elapsed = now.wrapping_sub(last);

            if elapsed >= self.delay_nanos as i64 {
                // Try to claim this slot
                if self.last_request.compare_exchange(last, now, ...).is_ok() {
                    return;
                }
                // CAS failed, retry
            } else {
                // Wait for cooldown
                let remaining = self.delay_nanos - elapsed as u64;
                tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_nanos(remaining)).await;
            }
        }
    }
}
```

This uses an atomic Compare-And-Swap (CAS) loop to coordinate concurrent access without locks.

# Extended Chapter 15: The Search System

## 15.A PostgreSQL Full-Text Search

Full-text search in PostgreSQL works by:

1. **Tokenization**: Breaking text into words
2. **Stemming**: Reducing words to their root form ("running" → "run")
3. **Removing stop words**: Ignoring common words like "the", "a", "is"
4. **Indexing**: Building an inverted index for fast lookup

### The tsvector Column

```sql
ALTER TABLE fic_info ADD COLUMN text_search tsvector;
```

A `tsvector` stores a sorted list of distinct lexemes (normalized words) with their positions.

### The tsquery Type

A `tsquery` represents a search query:

```sql
plainto_tsquery('english', 'harry potter')
-- Returns: 'harry' & 'potter'
```

### The @@ Operator

The `@@` operator checks if a document matches a query:

```sql
WHERE text_search @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'harry potter')
```

### Ranking

`ts_rank` computes a relevance score:

```sql
ts_rank(text_search, plainto_tsquery('english', 'harry potter')) AS rank
```

Higher rank means more relevant.

## 15.B The Search Query Builder

FicHub's search supports many parameters:

```rust
pub struct SearchParams {
    pub q: Option<String>,                    // Full-text search query
    pub include_tags: Vec<TagFilter>,          // Tags that ALL must be present
    pub exclude_tags: Vec<TagFilter>,          // Tags that NONE must be present
    pub include_any_tags: Vec<TagFilter>,      // Tags where at least ONE must be present
    pub min_words: Option<i64>,               // Minimum word count
    pub max_words: Option<i64>,               // Maximum word count
    pub min_chapters: Option<i32>,            // Minimum chapter count
    pub max_chapters: Option<i32>,            // Maximum chapter count
    pub complete: Option<bool>,               // Filter by completion status
    pub source: Option<String>,               // Filter by source site
    pub date_from: Option<DateTime<Utc>>,     // Filter by update date
    pub date_to: Option<DateTime<Utc>>,       // Filter by update date
    pub sort: Option<String>,                 // Sort order
    pub page: Option<usize>,                  // Page number
    pub per_page: Option<usize>,              // Results per page
}
```

The builder dynamically constructs SQL:

```rust
fn push_where_clauses(&self, qb: &mut QueryBuilder<Postgres>) {
    if let Some(ref q) = self.params.q {
        qb.push(" AND fi.text_search @@ plainto_tsquery('english', ");
        qb.push_bind(q);
        qb.push(")");
    }

    if let Some(min) = self.params.min_words {
        qb.push(" AND fi.words >= ");
        qb.push_bind(min);
    }

    // ... more clauses
}
```

## 15.C Batch Tag Fetching

After fetching search results, FicHub fetches tags for all results in a single query:

```rust
let url_ids: Vec<&str> = rows.iter().map(|r| r.id.as_str()).collect();
let tag_rows: Vec<TagDbRow> = sqlx::query_as::<_, TagDbRow>(
    r#"SELECT ft.url_id, t.name, t.tag_type_id, tt.name AS type_name, ft.score
       FROM fic_tags ft
       JOIN tags t ON t.id = ft.tag_id
       JOIN tag_types tt ON tt.id = t.tag_type_id
       WHERE ft.url_id = ANY($1)
         AND ft.score >= $2
       ORDER BY ft.url_id, ft.score DESC"#,
)
.bind(&url_ids)
.bind(state.config.tag_hidden_threshold)
.fetch_all(&state.db)
.await?;
```

This is much more efficient than fetching tags one story at a time (the N+1 problem).
