# The Proxy Pattern in Rate Limiting

The rate limiter uses the Proxy pattern:

```rust
pub rate_limiter: Box<dyn limiter::RateLimiter>,
```

The `Box<dyn RateLimiter>` is a trait object that proxies method calls to the actual implementation. This allows swapping implementations at runtime:

```rust
// Production: Redis-backed
let limiter = Box::new(RedisBucketLimiter::new(...));

// Testing: Mock
let limiter = Box::new(MockRateLimiter::new());
```

# The Chain of Responsibility in Error Handling

Error handling follows the Chain of Responsibility pattern:

```rust
impl From<sqlx::Error> for AppError {
    fn from(err: sqlx::Error) -> Self {
        AppError::Database(err.to_string())
    }
}

impl From<redis::RedisError> for AppError {
    fn from(err: redis::RedisError) -> Self {
        AppError::CacheError(err.to_string())
    }
}
```

Each `From` implementation converts one error type to `AppError`. The `?` operator tries each conversion in the chain until one matches.

---

# The Template Method Pattern in Scrapers

The SiteScraper trait defines a template:

```rust
#[async_trait]
pub trait SiteScraper: Send + Sync {
    fn can_handle(&self, url: &str) -> bool;
    async fn lookup(&self, client: &reqwest::Client, url: &str) -> Result<FicMetadata, ScrapeError>;
    async fn fetch_chapters(&self, client: &reqwest::Client, meta: &FicMetadata) -> Result<Vec<Chapter>, ScrapeError>;
    async fn extract_tags(&self, _client: &reqwest::Client, _url: &str) -> Result<Vec<ExtractedTag>, ScrapeError> {
        Ok(Vec::new())  // Default implementation
    }
}
```

The `extract_tags` method has a default implementation (Template Method), but scrapers can override it if they support tag extraction.

---

# The Facade Pattern in the Scraper Registry

The ScraperRegistry acts as a Facade:

```rust
impl ScraperRegistry {
    pub async fn lookup(&self, client: &reqwest::Client, url: &str) -> Result<FicMetadata, ScrapeError> {
        match self.find_scraper(url) {
            Some(scraper) => scraper.lookup(client, url).await,
            None => Err(ScrapeError::NotFound),
        }
    }
}
```

Instead of calling `find_scraper()` and then `lookup()` separately, callers can use the simplified `lookup()` method on the registry.

---

# The Composite Pattern in Router

The Axum router uses the Composite pattern:

```rust
Router::new()
    .route("/api/v0/epub", get(epub_handler))
    .route("/api/v0/meta", get(meta_handler))
    // ... more routes
```

Each `.route()` call adds a route to the router. The router itself is a composite of many routes, and the entire router can be treated as a single unit.

# The Null Object Pattern

FicHub uses the Null Object pattern in several places:

```rust
// Null tag extraction
async fn extract_tags(&self, _client: &reqwest::Client, _url: &str) -> Result<Vec<ExtractedTag>, ScrapeError> {
    Ok(Vec::new())  // Null implementation — returns empty
}
```

Scrapers that do not support tag extraction use the default (null) implementation instead of requiring every scraper to implement it.

# The Iterator Pattern in Tag Parsing

```rust
pub fn parse_tag_filters(input: &str) -> Result<Vec<TagFilter>, String> {
    let mut filters = Vec::new();
    for part in input.split(',') {
        let part = part.trim();
        if part.is_empty() { continue; }
        let colon_pos = part.find(':').ok_or_else(|| {
            format!("Invalid tag filter format '{}': expected 'type_id:name'", part)
        })?;
        let type_id: i16 = part[..colon_pos].parse()
            .map_err(|e| format!("Invalid tag_type_id: {}", e))?;
        let name = part[colon_pos + 1..].to_string();
        filters.push(TagFilter { tag_type_id: type_id, tag_name: name });
    }
    Ok(filters)
}
```

The iterator chain `split(',') → trim → filter → map → collect` processes each tag filter in a functional style.

---

# The State Pattern in Rate Limiting

The rate limiter has two states:

```rust
async fn check_ip(&self, ip: IpAddr) -> RateLimitResult {
    if !self.dynamic_rate_limit {
        // Static state: simple delay
        return RateLimitResult::Allowed;
    }

    // Dynamic state: token bucket
    if self.is_datacenter_ip(ip) {
        return RateLimitResult::Blocked;
    }

    let global_wait = self.check_bucket(...).await?;
    if global_wait > 0.0 {
        return RateLimitResult::Wait(global_wait);
    }

    let ip_wait = self.check_bucket(...).await?;
    if ip_wait > 0.0 {
        return RateLimitResult::Wait(ip_wait);
    }

    RateLimitResult::Allowed
}
```

The behavior changes based on the `dynamic_rate_limit` flag — this is the State pattern.

---

# The Object Pool Pattern in Database Connections

```rust
let pool = PgPoolOptions::new()
    .max_connections(20)
    .connect(database_url)
    .await?;
```

The connection pool maintains a pool of 20 connections. When a query needs a connection, it borrows one from the pool. When the query finishes, the connection returns to the pool. This is the Object Pool pattern — reusing expensive resources instead of creating new ones each time.

# The Command Pattern in Background Jobs

The collection worker uses the Command pattern:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct QueueItem {
    pub url_id: String,
    pub site_domain: String,
    pub site_work_id: String,
}
```

Each `QueueItem` encapsulates a command to be executed. The worker loop dequeues items and executes them:

```rust
if let Some(item_str) = item_str {
    match serde_json::from_str::<QueueItem>(&item_str) {
        Ok(item) => {
            if let Err(e) = self.process_work(item).await {
                error!("Error processing work on {}: {}", domain, e);
            }
        }
        Err(e) => warn!("Invalid queue item: {}", e),
    }
}
```

# The Mediator Pattern in AppState

AppState acts as a Mediator:

```rust
pub struct AppState {
    pub config: Config,
    pub db: sqlx::PgPool,
    pub redis: redis::aio::MultiplexedConnection,
    pub http_client: reqwest::Client,
    pub scraper_registry: Arc<ScraperRegistry>,
    pub cache_semaphores: CacheSemaphores,
    pub rate_limiter: Box<dyn limiter::RateLimiter>,
    pub recommender_engine: RecommendationEngine,
    pub collection_worker: CollectionWorker,
}
```

Instead of components communicating directly with each other, they all go through AppState. This reduces coupling and makes the system easier to understand and modify.

# The Memento Pattern in Configuration

The Config struct captures a snapshot of the system's configuration:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]

    pub database_url: String,
    pub redis_url: String,
    // ... 30+ fields
}
```

The `Clone` derive allows creating copies of the configuration at any time, preserving the state as it was when loaded.

# The Flyweight Pattern in ExtractedTag

The ExtractedTag constructors create lightweight, reusable tag objects:

```rust
impl ExtractedTag {
    pub fn fandom(name: &str) -> Self { Self { name: name.to_string(), tag_type_id: 1 } }
    pub fn character(name: &str) -> Self { Self { name: name.to_string(), tag_type_id: 2 } }
    pub fn freeform(name: &str) -> Self { Self { name: name.to_string(), tag_type_id: 4 } }
}
```

These factory methods make it easy to create correctly-typed tags without remembering the numeric type IDs.

# The Adapter Pattern in Error Conversion

The `From` implementations act as Adapters:

```rust
impl From<sqlx::Error> for AppError {

        AppError::Database(err.to_string())
    }
}
```

This adapts `sqlx::Error` to `AppError`, allowing seamless integration between the database layer and the application layer.

# The Bridge Pattern in EType

The EType enum bridges the concept of export types with their concrete implementations:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Hash, Eq, PartialEq)]
pub enum EType {
    Epub, Html, Mobi, Pdf,
}

impl EType {
    pub fn as_str(&self) -> &'static str { ... }
    pub fn suffix(&self) -> &'static str { ... }

}
```

Each variant maps to string representations, file suffixes, and version numbers — bridging the abstract concept with concrete values.

# The Factory Pattern in ScraperRegistry

```rust
impl ScraperRegistry {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        let mut scrapers: Vec<Box<dyn SiteScraper>> = Vec::new();
        scrapers.push(Box::new(sites::ao3::Ao3Scraper));
```

# The Iterator Pattern in Batch Tag Fetching

```rust
let url_ids: Vec<&str> = rows.iter().map(|r| r.id.as_str()).collect();
```

The iterator chain `iter() → map() → collect()` transforms the rows into a list of URL IDs for batch processing.

# The Observer Pattern in Tracing

The tracing system observes all events:

```rust
tracing::info!("Starting fichub-rs server on port {}", config.app_port);
tracing::debug!("Extracted {} tags for {}", tags.len(), url_id);
tracing::error!("Internal error: {}", msg);
```

Each log call is an event that is observed by the tracing subscriber, which decides what to do with it (print to console, write to file, send to external service, etc.).

# The Null Object Pattern in Recommendations

When recommendations cannot be computed, the engine returns an empty vector:

```rust
pub async fn get_recommendations(&self, query: &RecQuery, config: &Config) -> Result<Vec<RecResult>, AppError> {
    let limit = query.n.min(config.rec_max_recommendations);
    if limit == 0 {
        return Ok(Vec::new());  // Null result — empty but not an error
    }
    // ...
}
```

This is the Null Object pattern — returning an empty result instead of an error when there is nothing to return.

# The Prototype Pattern in FicMetadata

The FicMetadata struct serves as a prototype that all scrapers produce:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct FicMetadata {
    pub url_id: String,
    pub title: String,
    pub author: String,
    pub chapters: i32,
    pub words: i64,
    pub desc: String,
    pub published: i64,
    pub updated: i64,
    pub status: String,
    pub source: String,
    pub source_id: i64,
    pub author_id: i64,
    pub author_url: String,
    pub author_local_id: String,
    pub content_hash: Option<String>,
    pub extra_meta: Option<String>,
    pub raw_extended_meta: Option<String>,
}
```

Every scraper produces this same structure, regardless of the source website. This allows the rest of the system to work with a uniform interface.

# The Chain Pattern in URL ID Generation

```rust
pub fn generate_url_id(source_id: i64, story_id: &str) -> String {
    use sha2::{Sha256, Digest};
    let mut hasher = Sha256::new();
    hasher.update(source_id.to_string().as_bytes());
    hasher.update(b":");
    hasher.update(story_id.as_bytes());
    let result = hasher.finalize();
    hex::encode(&result[..6])
}
```

This chains together: source_id → colon separator → story_id → SHA-256 hash → first 12 hex characters.

# The Proxy Pattern in Rate Limit Check

```rust
async fn check_ip(&self, ip: IpAddr) -> RateLimitResult {
    if !self.dynamic_rate_limit {
        let delay = self.static_delay_base + rand::random::<f64>() * self.static_delay_base;
        tokio::time::sleep(tokio::time::Duration::from_secs_f64(delay)).await;
        return RateLimitResult::Allowed;
    }
    // ... dynamic rate limiting
}
```

The `check_ip` method acts as a proxy, deciding which rate limiting strategy to use based on configuration.

# The Facade Pattern in Server Initialization

```rust
    let redis_client = redis::Client::open(config.redis_url.as_str()).expect("...");

    let scraper_registry = Arc::new(ScraperRegistry::new());

    // ... start serving
}
```

The `run()` function is a Facade that hides the complexity of initializing all the subsystems.

# The Template Method in Export

The export handler follows a template:

```rust
pub async fn epub_handler(...) -> Result<Json<Value>, AppError> {
    // Step 1: Validate input
    let query = params.q.as_deref().unwrap_or("");

    // Step 2: Find scraper
    let scraper = state.scraper_registry.find_scraper(query)...;

    // Step 3: Lookup metadata
    let meta = scraper.lookup(&state.http_client, query).await...;

    // Step 4: Store in database
    queries::upsert_fic_info(&state.db, &fic_info_row).await?;

    // Step 5: Check blacklists
    let fic_blacklist = queries::check_fic_blacklist(&state.db, &meta.url_id).await?;

    // Step 6: Check cache
    let cached = queries::find_export_log(&state.db, ...).await?;
    if cached.is_some() {
        return Ok(build_response(&cached.unwrap()));
    }

    // Step 7: Acquire semaphore
    let sem = cache::get_export_semaphore(...).await;
    let _permit = sem.acquire().await?;

    // Step 8: Double-check cache
    let cached = queries::find_export_log(&state.db, ...).await?;
    if cached.is_some() {
        return Ok(build_response(&cached.unwrap()));
    }

    // Step 9: Fetch chapters
    let chapters = scraper.fetch_chapters(&state.http_client, &meta).await...;

    // Step 10: Generate EPUB
    let (epub_path, hash) = export::epub::create_epub(&meta, &chapters, &state.config.tmp_dir).await...;

    // Step 11: Cache the file
    let dest = cache::disk::cache_path(&state.config.cache_dir, &EType::Epub, &meta.url_id, &hash);
    cache::disk::move_to_cache(&epub_path, &dest)?;

    // Step 12: Record in database
    queries::insert_export_log(&state.db, &meta.url_id, version, "epub", &input_hash, &hash).await?;

    // Step 13: Return response
    Ok(Json(json!({ "err": 0, "url_id": meta.url_id, "epub_url": format!("/cache/epub/{}?h={}", meta.url_id, hash) })))
}
```

This template is followed for every export request, with variations for different formats.

# The Chain of Responsibility in Error Handling

```rust
// In epub_handler:
let scraper = state.scraper_registry.find_scraper(query)
    .ok_or_else(|| AppError::BadRequest(-5, format!("unsupported URL: {}", query)))?;

let meta = scraper.lookup(&state.http_client, query).await
    .map_err(|e| AppError::ScrapeError(e.to_string()))?;

queries::upsert_fic_info(&state.db, &fic_info_row).await?;

let chapters = scraper.fetch_chapters(&state.http_client, &meta).await
    .map_err(|e| AppError::ScrapeError(e.to_string()))?;
```

Each step can fail, and the `?` operator propagates the error up the chain. The `From` implementations convert different error types to `AppError`.

# The Command Pattern in Collection Worker

```rust
pub async fn run(&self) {
    loop {
        for fetcher in &self.fetchers {
            let item_str: Option<String> = {
                let mut conn = self.redis.lock().await;
                redis::cmd("LPOP").arg(&key).query_async(&mut *conn).await.unwrap_or(None)
            };

            if let Some(item_str) = item_str {
                match serde_json::from_str::<QueueItem>(&item_str) {
                    Ok(item) => {
                        if let Err(e) = self.process_work(item).await {
                            error!("Error: {}", e);
                        }
                    }
                    Err(e) => warn!("Invalid: {}", e),
                }
            }
        }
        tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(100)).await;
    }
}
```

Each QueueItem is a Command that encapsulates a unit of work to be executed.

# The Template Pattern in Rate Limiting

Both global and per-IP rate limiting follow the same template:

1. Check the bucket
2. If wait time > 0, return Wait
3. If wait time <= 0, return Allowed

```rust
let global_wait = self.check_bucket("rate:global", self.global_capacity, self.global_flow)
    .await.unwrap_or(-1.0);
if global_wait > 0.0 {
    return RateLimitResult::Wait(global_wait.ceil() as u64);
}

let ip_wait = self.check_bucket(&ip_key, self.ip_capacity, self.ip_flow)
    .await.unwrap_or(-1.0);
if ip_wait > 0.0 {
    return RateLimitResult::Wait(ip_wait.ceil() as u64);
}
```

The template is the same; only the bucket parameters differ.

# The Strategy Pattern in Cache Management

Different cache operations use different strategies:

- **EPUB**: Generated and cached on disk
- **HTML**: Generated and cached as ZIP
- **MOBI/PDF**: Converted from cached EPUB via Calibre
- **Metadata**: Always fetched fresh (not cached)

Each format has its own caching strategy.

# The Template Method in Search

Both count and data queries follow the same template:

1. Start with base SELECT
2. Push WHERE clauses
3. Add ORDER BY
4. Add LIMIT/OFFSET (data only)

```rust
pub fn build_count_query(&self) -> QueryBuilder<Postgres> {
    let mut qb = QueryBuilder::new("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM fic_info fi WHERE 1=1");
    self.push_where_clauses(&mut qb);
    qb
}

pub fn build_data_query(&self) -> QueryBuilder<Postgres> {
    let mut qb = QueryBuilder::new("SELECT fi.* FROM fic_info fi WHERE 1=1");
    self.push_where_clauses(&mut qb);
    // ... add ORDER BY, LIMIT, OFFSET
    qb
}
```

The `push_where_clauses` method is the Template Method, reused by both queries.

# The Adapter Pattern in Tag Resolution

```rust
pub async fn resolve_tag(pool: &PgPool, tag_name: &str, tag_type_id: i16) -> AppResult<TagResolution> {
    // Step 1: Try exact match
    if let Some(row) = lookup_tag(pool, tag_name).await? {
        return Ok(TagResolution { tag_id: row.0, tag_name: row.1, tag_type_id: row.2, is_new: false });
    }

    // Step 2: Try alias
    if let Some(canonical_id) = lookup_alias(pool, tag_name).await? {
        let tag = lookup_tag_by_id(pool, canonical_id).await?...;
        return Ok(TagResolution { tag_id: tag.0, tag_name: tag.1, tag_type_id: tag.2, is_new: false });
    }

    // Step 3: Create new
    let new_id = create_tag(pool, tag_name, tag_type_id).await?;
    Ok(TagResolution { tag_id: new_id, tag_name: tag_name.to_string(), tag_type_id, is_new: true })
}
```

This adapts three different data sources (exact match, alias, new tag creation) to a uniform TagResolution output.

# The Template Method in Tag Processing

Every tag operation follows the same template:

1. Validate input
2. Check rate limit
3. Verify fic exists
4. Perform the operation
5. Return response

```rust
pub async fn submit_tag(State(state), ConnectInfo(remote), Json(body)) -> Result<Json<Value>, AppError> {
    // 1. Validate
    if body.url_id.is_empty() || body.tag_name.is_empty() {
        return Ok(Json(json!({"err": -1, "msg": "required"})));
    }

    // 2. Rate limit
    check_tag_rate_limit(&mut redis, "submit", ip, limit).await?;

    // 3. Verify
    let exists = sqlx::query_scalar("SELECT EXISTS(...)").fetch_one(&state.db).await?;
    if !exists {
        return Ok(Json(json!({"err": -5, "msg": "not found"})));
    }

    // 4. Perform
    let resolution = resolve::resolve_tag(&state.db, &body.tag_name, body.tag_type_id).await?;
    sqlx::query("INSERT INTO fic_tags ...").execute(&state.db).await?;

    // 5. Return
    Ok(Json(json!({"err": 0, "tag_id": resolution.tag_id})))
}
```

# The Composite Pattern in Recommendation Scoring

The final recommendation score is a composite of multiple factors:

```
final_score = collab_score * weight + tag_score * (1.0 - weight)
final_score *= boost
```

Where:
- `collab_score` = co-occurrence Jaccard similarity
- `tag_score` = tag-based similarity
- `weight` = based on favouriter count
- `boost` = community voting boost

The search system supports multiple sorting strategies:

- Relevance (when search query is present)
- Date (when no search query)
- Word count
- Chapter count
- Title

Each strategy is implemented as a match arm in the sort logic.

# The Template Method in Cache Download

Both download handlers follow the same template:

1. Parse request parameters
2. Find the cache file
3. Validate the hash
4. Serve the file

```rust
pub async fn download_with_hash(State(state), Path(...), Query(params)) -> Response {
    // 1. Parse
    let etype = etype_str.parse::<EType>()?;
    let hash = params.h.unwrap_or_else(|| fname.trim_end_matches(etype.suffix()));

    // 2. Find
    let cache_path = cache::disk::cache_path(&state.config.cache_dir, &etype, &url_id, &hash);
    if !cache_path.exists() {
        return Json(json!({"err": -5, "msg": "not found"}));
    }

    // 3. Validate
    let actual_hash = cache::disk::file_md5(&cache_path)?;
    if actual_hash != hash {
        return Json(json!({"err": -5, "msg": "hash mismatch"}));
    }

    // 4. Serve
    let data = tokio::fs::read(&cache_path).await?;
    (headers, data).into_response()
}
```

# The Strategy Pattern in Error Responses

Different error types produce different HTTP responses:

```rust
AppError::BadRequest(code, msg) => (StatusCode::BAD_REQUEST, json!({"err": code, "msg": msg}))
AppError::RateLimited(retry_after) => (StatusCode::TOO_MANY_REQUESTS, json!({...}))
AppError::NotFound(msg) => (StatusCode::NOT_FOUND, json!({"err": -5, "msg": msg}))
AppError::Internal(msg) => (StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, json!({"err": -1, "msg": "internal error"}))
```

Each error variant is a strategy for producing an HTTP response.

# The Template Method in Tag Resolution

Tag resolution follows a template:

1. Try exact match
2. Try alias lookup
3. Create new tag

```rust
pub async fn resolve_tag(pool: &PgPool, tag_name: &str, tag_type_id: i16) -> AppResult<TagResolution> {
    // Template: try → try → create
    if let Some(row) = lookup_tag(pool, tag_name).await? { return Ok(...); }
    if let Some(id) = lookup_alias(pool, tag_name).await? { return Ok(...); }
    let new_id = create_tag(pool, tag_name, tag_type_id).await?;
    Ok(TagResolution { ... })
}
```

# The Strategy Pattern in Sort Order

```rust
match sort {
    "-relevance" => qb.push("rank DESC"),
    "-date" => qb.push("fi.fic_updated DESC"),
    "-words" => qb.push("fi.words DESC"),
    "-chapters" => qb.push("fi.chapters DESC"),
    "-title" => qb.push("fi.title ASC"),
    _ => qb.push("fi.fic_updated DESC"),
}
```

Each sort option is a strategy for ordering search results.

# The Complete Guide to FicHub's Database Layer

## Understanding the Database Schema

FicHub's database is the backbone of the entire system. Every piece of data — from story metadata to user votes to cached exports — is stored in PostgreSQL. Let us examine every table in complete detail.

### The fic_info Table

This is the most important table. It stores metadata about every fanfiction story that FicHub has ever processed.

```sql
CREATE TABLE fic_info (
    id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    created TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
    title TEXT NOT NULL,
    author TEXT NOT NULL,
    author_url TEXT,
    author_local_id TEXT,
    chapters INT DEFAULT 1,
    words BIGINT DEFAULT 0,
    description TEXT DEFAULT '',
    fic_created TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    fic_updated TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    status TEXT DEFAULT 'ongoing',
    source TEXT NOT NULL,
    extra_meta JSONB,
    raw_extended_meta TEXT,
    source_id INT,
    author_id INT,
    content_hash TEXT,
    text_search tsvector
);
```

Let us understand each column:

**id**: The unique identifier for the story. This is a 12-character hex string generated by hashing the source_id and story_id together. For example, AO3 story 123456 might get the id `a1b2c3d4e5f6`.

**created**: When this record was first created in FicHub's database. Uses TIMESTAMPTZ (timestamp with time zone) for timezone safety.

**updated**: When this record was last modified. Updated every time the story metadata is refreshed.

**title**: The story's title as it appears on the source site.

**author**: The author's display name.

**author_url**: The author's profile URL on the source site. For AO3, this would be something like `https://archiveofourown.org/users/AuthorName`.

**author_local_id**: The author's ID on the source site. This is used to generate URLs and is site-specific.

**chapters**: The total number of chapters. Note that this might be 1 for single-chapter stories or the planned chapter count for works in progress.

**words**: The total word count. Stored as BIGINT because some stories have millions of words.

**description**: The story's summary/description as it appears on the source site. May contain HTML.

**fic_created**: When the story was originally published on the source site.

**fic_updated**: When the story was last updated on the source site.

**status**: One of: "ongoing" (still being written), "complete" (finished), "hiatus" (on break), or "cancelled" (abandoned).

**source**: The full URL of the story on the source site.

**extra_meta**: Additional metadata stored as JSON. This might include ratings, categories, or other site-specific information.

**raw_extended_meta**: Raw metadata from the source site, stored as text.

**source_id**: The numeric ID of the source site (1=AO3, 2=FF.net, etc.).

**author_id**: The author's numeric ID on the source site.

**content_hash**: A hash of the story's content, used for cache invalidation. When the story is updated, this hash changes, forcing cached exports to be regenerated.

**text_search**: A PostgreSQL tsvector column for full-text search. Automatically updated by a trigger when title, author, or description changes.

### The tags Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE tags (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE COLLATE "C",
    tag_type_id SMALLINT NOT NULL
);
```

**id**: Auto-incrementing integer ID.

**name**: The tag name, stored with case-sensitive collation (COLLATE "C"). This means "Harry Potter" and "harry potter" are different tags.

**tag_type_id**: The type of tag:
- 1: Fandom (e.g., "Harry Potter")
- 2: Character (e.g., "Hermione Granger")
- 3: Relationship (e.g., "Harry/Hermione")
- 4: Freeform (e.g., "Fluff", "Angst")
- 5: Warning (e.g., "Major Character Death")
- 6: Category (e.g., "M/M")
- 7: Rating (e.g., "Explicit")

### The tag_aliases Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE tag_aliases (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    alias_name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    canonical_tag_id INT NOT NULL REFERENCES tags(id)
);
```

This allows alternative names to point to canonical tags. For example:
- "hp" → "Harry Potter"
- "hermione" → "Hermione Jean Granger"

### The fic_tags Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE fic_tags (
    url_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES fic_info(id),
    tag_id INT NOT NULL REFERENCES tags(id),
    added_by_ip INET,
    score SMALLINT DEFAULT 0,
    PRIMARY KEY (url_id, tag_id)
);
```

This links stories to tags. The composite primary key `(url_id, tag_id)` ensures each story-tag pair is unique.

### The fic_tag_votes Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE fic_tag_votes (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    url_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    tag_id INT NOT NULL,
    voter_ip INET NOT NULL,
    value SMALLINT NOT NULL CHECK (value IN (-1, 1)),
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
    UNIQUE (url_id, tag_id, voter_ip)
);
```

Each vote is tied to an IP address (since FicHub does not require user accounts). The UNIQUE constraint ensures each IP can only vote once per story-tag pair.

### The tag_flags Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE tag_flags (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    url_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    tag_id INT NOT NULL,
    flagged_by_ip INET NOT NULL,
    reason TEXT,
    resolved BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
    UNIQUE (url_id, tag_id, flagged_by_ip)
);
```

Flags allow users to report inappropriate tags. The `resolved` field tracks whether a curator has reviewed the flag.

### The export_log Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE export_log (
    url_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    version INT NOT NULL,
    etype TEXT NOT NULL,
    input_hash TEXT NOT NULL,
    export_hash TEXT NOT NULL,
    created TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
    PRIMARY KEY (url_id, version, etype, input_hash)
);
```

This tracks which files have been generated. The composite primary key includes the version and input hash, allowing for cache invalidation when stories are updated.

### The request_source Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE request_source (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    created TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
    is_automated BOOLEAN,
    route TEXT,
    description TEXT,
    UNIQUE (is_automated, route, description)
);
```

Tracks where API requests come from. The UNIQUE constraint ensures each source combination is stored only once.

### The request_log Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE request_log (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    created TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
    source_id INT REFERENCES request_source(id),
    etype TEXT,
    query TEXT,
    info_request_ms INT,
    url_id TEXT,
    fic_info TEXT,
    export_ms INT,
    export_file_name TEXT,
    export_file_hash TEXT,
    url TEXT
);
```

Logs every API request with timing information. This is invaluable for debugging performance issues.

### The fic_blacklist Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE fic_blacklist (
    url_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    created TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
    reason INT NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (url_id, reason)
);
```

Blacklisted stories. The reason codes:
- 5: Hard blacklist (story is completely blocked)
- 6: Greylist (metadata shown, downloads blocked)
- 7: Hard blacklist
- 8: Hard blacklist

### The author_blacklist Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE author_blacklist (
    source_id INT NOT NULL,
    author_id INT NOT NULL,
    created TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
    reason INT NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (source_id, author_id, reason)
);
```

Blacklisted authors. All stories by this author are blocked.

### The fic_version_bump Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE fic_version_bump (
    id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    value INT DEFAULT 0
);
```

Used for cache invalidation. When a story is updated, its version bump is incremented, which changes the cache version and forces regeneration of all cached exports.

### The fic_works Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE fic_works (
    url_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES fic_info(id),
    site_domain TEXT,
    site_work_id TEXT,
    favouriter_count INT DEFAULT 0,
    first_favourite_scraped TIMESTAMPTZ,
    last_favourite_scraped TIMESTAMPTZ
);
```

Extended metadata for the recommendation engine. Tracks how many users have favourited each work.

### The fic_bookmarks Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE fic_bookmarks (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    user_hash TEXT NOT NULL,
    url_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES fic_info(id),
    site_domain TEXT,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
    UNIQUE (user_hash, url_id)
);
```

Records which users have favourited which stories. The user_hash is a SHA-256 hash of the user's profile URL.

### The fic_bookmark_cooccur Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE fic_bookmark_cooccur (
    work_a TEXT NOT NULL,
    work_b TEXT NOT NULL,
    cooccur_count INT DEFAULT 1,
    last_updated TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
    PRIMARY KEY (work_a, work_b)
);
```

Tracks how many users have favourited both of two stories. This is the foundation of the collaborative filtering recommendation engine.

### The precomputed_recommendations Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE precomputed_recommendations (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    url_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    recommended_url_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    score REAL,
    rank SMALLINT,
    computed_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
);
```

Caches precomputed recommendations for popular stories. The TTL is controlled by `rec_cache_ttl_hours`.

### The recommendation_suggestions Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE recommendation_suggestions (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    url_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    suggested_url_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    suggested_by_ip INET,
    comment TEXT,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
);
```

User-submitted recommendation suggestions.

### The recommendation_votes Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE recommendation_votes (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    suggestion_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES recommendation_suggestions(id),
    voter_ip INET NOT NULL,
    vote SMALLINT NOT NULL CHECK (vote IN (-1, 1)),
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
    UNIQUE (suggestion_id, voter_ip)
);
```

Votes on recommendation suggestions.

### The tag_types Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE tag_types (
    id SMALLINT PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
);
```

Lookup table for tag type names.

# The Complete Guide to FicHub's Export System

## How EPUB Generation Works

The EPUB format is complex, but the `epub-builder` crate handles most of the complexity. Let us walk through the complete process:

### Step 1: Create Work Directory

```rust
let uuid = Uuid::new_v4();
let work_dir = tmp_dir.join(uuid.to_string());
fs::create_dir_all(&work_dir)?;
```

Each export gets its own temporary directory to prevent conflicts.

### Step 2: Initialize Builder

```rust
let mut builder = EpubBuilder::new(ZipLibrary::new()?)?;
```

The `ZipLibrary` provides ZIP compression, which is required by the EPUB format.

### Step 3: Set Metadata

```rust
builder.metadata("title", &meta.title)?;
builder.metadata("author", &meta.author)?;
builder.metadata("lang", "en")?;
builder.metadata("description", &meta.desc)?;
```

These become the Dublin Core metadata in the EPUB file.

### Step 4: Add Stylesheet

```rust
let css = concat!(
    "body{font-family:serif;line-height:1.5;}",
    "h2{text-align:center;}",
    "p{margin:0.5em 0;}"
);
builder.stylesheet(css.as_bytes())?;
```

The CSS provides basic formatting for the e-book.

### Step 5: Add Introduction

```rust
let intro_html = format!(
    r#"<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">
<head><title>Introduction</title>
<link rel="stylesheet" type="text/css" href="stylesheet.css"/>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>{title}</h1>
    <h2>by {author}</h2>
    <table>
        <tr><td>Words:</td><td>{words}</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Chapters:</td><td>{chapters}</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Status:</td><td>{status}</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Published:</td><td>{published}</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Updated:</td><td>{updated}</td></tr>
    </table>
    <hr/>
    <p>{desc}</p>
</body>
</html>"#,
    // ... format parameters
);
builder.add_content(EpubContent::new("introduction.xhtml", intro_html.as_bytes())
    .title("Introduction"))?;
```

The introduction page shows the story's metadata.

### Step 6: Add Chapters

```rust
for chapter in chapters {
    let chapter_html = format!(
        r#"<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">
<head><title>{title}</title>
<link rel="stylesheet" type="text/css" href="stylesheet.css"/>
</head>
<body>
    <h2>{title}</h2>
    {content}
</body>
</html>"#,
        title = escape_html(&chapter.title),
        content = chapter.content,
    );
    let filename = format!("chapter_{}.xhtml", chapter.chapter_id);
    builder.add_content(EpubContent::new(filename.as_str(), chapter_html.as_bytes())
        .title(&chapter.title))?;
}
```

Each chapter becomes a separate XHTML file in the EPUB.

### Step 7: Generate File

```rust
let epub_path = work_dir.join("output.epub");
let file = fs::File::create(&epub_path)?;
builder.generate(file)?;
```

The `generate` method writes the complete EPUB file.

### Step 8: Compute Hash

```rust
let epub_data = fs::read(&epub_path)?;
let md5_hex = Md5::digest(&epub_data)
    .iter()
    .map(|b| format!("{:02x}", b))
    .collect::<String>();
```

The MD5 hash is used as the cache key.

## How HTML Bundle Generation Works

The HTML bundle is simpler than EPUB but follows a similar pattern:

### Step 1: Build Navigation

```rust
let mut chapters_nav = String::new();
for chapter in chapters {
    chapters_nav.push_str(&format!(
        r##"<li><a href="#ch{ch}">{title}</a></li>"##,
        ch = chapter.chapter_id,
        title = escape_html(&chapter.title),
    ));
}
```

### Step 2: Build Content

```rust
let mut chapters_content = String::new();
for chapter in chapters {
    chapters_content.push_str(&format!(
        r#"<h2 id="ch{ch}">{title}</h2>
{content}"#,
        ch = chapter.chapter_id,
        title = escape_html(&chapter.title),
        content = chapter.content,
    ));
}
```

### Step 3: Assemble HTML

The complete HTML includes:
- Responsive CSS
- Metadata header
- Chapter navigation
- All chapter content
- Footer

### Step 4: ZIP and Hash

The HTML file is compressed into a ZIP archive and its MD5 hash is computed.

## How Format Conversion Works

MOBI and PDF conversion uses Calibre's `ebook-convert` tool:

```rust
// Option 1: Direct execution
Command::new("ebook-convert")
    .arg(epub_path)
    .arg(output_path)
    .output()
    .await

// Option 2: Docker execution
Command::new("docker")
    .arg("exec")
    .arg(container)
    .arg("ebook-convert")
    .arg(epub_path)
    .arg(output_path)
    .output()
    .await
```

The conversion is wrapped in a 300-second timeout and retried once on failure.

# The Complete Guide to FicHub's Rate Limiting

## The Token Bucket Algorithm

The token bucket is one of the most elegant rate limiting algorithms. Let us understand it completely.

### The Concept

Imagine a bucket that holds tokens:
- Tokens are added at a constant rate (the "flow rate")
- The bucket has a maximum capacity
- Each request consumes one token
- If the bucket is empty, the request must wait

### The Parameters

FicHub uses two buckets:

**Global Bucket:**
- Capacity: 150 tokens
- Flow rate: 30 tokens/second
- This allows bursts of up to 150 requests, then sustains 30/second

**Per-IP Bucket:**
- Capacity: 30 tokens
- Flow rate: ~0.116 tokens/second (1 token per ~8.6 seconds)
- This limits each IP to about 7 requests per minute

### The Lua Script

The algorithm is implemented in Lua for atomic execution in Redis:

```lua
-- Read current state
local bucket = redis.call('HMGET', key, 'value', 'last_drain')
local value = tonumber(bucket[1])
local last_drain = tonumber(bucket[2])

-- Get current time from Redis server
local now = redis.call('TIME')
local now_sec = tonumber(now[1]) + tonumber(now[2])/1000000

-- Initialize if first request
if value == nil then
    value = capacity
    last_drain = now_sec
    redis.call('HMSET', key, 'value', value, 'last_drain', last_drain)
end

-- Calculate available tokens
local elapsed = now_sec - last_drain
local new_tokens = math.min(capacity, value + elapsed * flow)
local allowed = new_tokens - requested

if allowed >= 0 then
    -- Enough tokens: deduct and update
    redis.call('HMSET', key, 'value', allowed, 'last_drain', now_sec)
    return -1  -- -1 means "allowed"
else
    -- Not enough tokens: calculate wait time
    local wait = (requested - new_tokens) / flow
    return wait  -- Positive number = seconds to wait
end
```

### Why Lua?

The entire script runs as a single atomic operation in Redis. This prevents race conditions where two concurrent requests might both see enough tokens and both proceed.

### The Failure Penalty

When a request fails (e.g., scraping error), the rate limiter penalizes the IP:

```rust
async fn penalize(&self, key: &str, capacity: f64, flow: f64) -> Result<(), redis::RedisError> {
    let _: f64 = redis::cmd("EVALSHA")
        .arg(&self.lua_sha[..])
        .arg(1)
        .arg(key)
        .arg(1.5)  // Penalize with 1.5 tokens instead of 1
        .arg(capacity)
        .arg(flow)
        .query_async(&mut conn)
        .await?;
    Ok(())
}
```

This consumes extra tokens, slowing down future requests from that IP.

# The Complete Guide to FicHub's Recommendation Engine

## How Collaborative Filtering Works

Collaborative filtering is based on a simple insight: people who liked the same things in the past will probably like similar things in the future.

### The Data Collection Phase

The collection worker scrapes user favourites from fanfiction sites:

1. For a given story, find all users who favourited it
2. For each user, find all their other favourites
3. Record which stories co-occur (appear together in the same user's favourites)

### The Co-occurrence Matrix

The co-occurrence table tracks how many users favourited both of two stories:

```
Story A: favouriters = {User1, User2, User3}
Story B: favouriters = {User1, User2, User4}
Story C: favouriters = {User1, User3}

Co-occurrence:
A-B: 2 (User1, User2)
A-C: 2 (User1, User3)
B-C: 1 (User1)
```

### The Jaccard Similarity

To compare how similar two stories are, FicHub uses the Jaccard index:

```
Jaccard(A, B) = |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|
```

For stories A and B:
- A has 3 favouriters
- B has 3 favouriters
- 2 users favourited both
- Jaccard = 2 / (3 + 3 - 2) = 2/4 = 0.5

### The Score Blending

For stories with few favouriters, collaborative filtering is unreliable. FicHub blends it with tag-based similarity:

```
weight = min(1.0, favouriter_count / 5.0)
final_score = collab_score * weight + tag_score * (1.0 - weight)
```

If a story has 5+ favouriters, collaborative filtering dominates. If fewer, tag-based similarity is used more.

### The Community Boost

Users can upvote or downvote recommendations:

```
boost = 1.0 + gamma * ln(1 + max(0, net_votes))
final_score *= boost
```

The `gamma` parameter (default 0.2) controls how much community votes affect the ranking.

### The Precomputation Cache

For popular stories, recommendations are precomputed and cached in the `precomputed_recommendations` table. The cache TTL is controlled by `rec_cache_ttl_hours`.

# The Complete Guide to FicHub's Search System

## PostgreSQL Full-Text Search

Full-text search in PostgreSQL is powerful and efficient. Here is how it works:

### The tsvector Column

A tsvector stores a normalized representation of text:

```sql
SELECT to_tsvector('english', 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog');
-- Returns: 'brown':3 'dog':9 'fox':4 'jump':5 'lazi':8 'quick':2
```

Notice how "jumps" becomes "jump" (stemmed) and "lazy" becomes "lazi" (stemmed).

### The tsquery Type

A tsquery represents a search expression:

```sql
SELECT plainto_tsquery('english', 'quick fox');
-- Returns: 'quick' & 'fox'
```

The `&` means AND — both terms must be present.

### The @@ Operator

The @@ operator checks if a document matches a query:

```sql
WHERE text_search @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'quick fox')
```

### Ranking

`ts_rank` computes a relevance score:

```sql
ts_rank(text_search, plainto_tsquery('english', 'quick fox')) AS rank
```

Higher rank means more relevant.

### The GIN Index

A GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) makes text searches fast:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_fic_info_text_search ON fic_info USING gin(text_search);
```

Without this index, every search would scan the entire table.

### The Trigger

A PostgreSQL trigger automatically updates the tsvector column when title, author, or description changes:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION update_fic_info_text_search() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
    NEW.text_search :=
        setweight(to_tsvector('english', COALESCE(NEW.title, '')), 'A') ||
        setweight(to_tsvector('english', COALESCE(NEW.author, '')), 'B') ||
        setweight(to_tsvector('english', COALESCE(NEW.description, '')), 'C');
    RETURN NEW;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;
```

The weights (A, B, C) affect ranking — title matches are more relevant than description matches.

## The Search Query Builder

The SearchQueryBuilder dynamically constructs SQL based on search parameters:

### Base Query

```rust
let mut qb = QueryBuilder::<Postgres>::new("SELECT fi.* FROM fic_info fi WHERE 1=1");
```

### Full-Text Search

```rust
if let Some(ref q) = self.params.q {
    qb.push(" AND fi.text_search @@ plainto_tsquery('english', ");
    qb.push_bind(q);
    qb.push(")");
}
```

### Tag Filters

Each tag filter adds an EXISTS subquery:

```rust
for tag in &self.params.include_tags {
    qb.push(" AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fic_tags ft");
    qb.push(" JOIN tags t ON t.id = ft.tag_id");
    qb.push(" WHERE ft.url_id = fi.id");
    qb.push(" AND t.name = ");
    qb.push_bind(&tag.tag_name);
    qb.push(")");
}
```

### Numeric Filters

```rust
if let Some(min) = self.params.min_words {
    qb.push(" AND fi.words >= ");
    qb.push_bind(min);
}
```

### Sort Order

```rust
match sort {
    "-relevance" => qb.push("rank DESC"),
    "-date" => qb.push("fi.fic_updated DESC"),
    "-words" => qb.push("fi.words DESC"),
    // ...
}
```

### Pagination

```rust
let page = self.params.page.unwrap_or(1).max(1);
let per_page = self.params.per_page.unwrap_or(20).max(1);
let offset = (page - 1) * per_page;
qb.push(" LIMIT ");
qb.push_bind(per_page as i64);
qb.push(" OFFSET ");
qb.push_bind(offset as i64);
```

# The Complete Guide to FicHub's OPDS Catalog

## What is OPDS?

OPDS (Open Publication Distribution System) is a standard for distributing e-books. It allows e-readers to browse and download books from online catalogs.

## How OPDS Feeds Work

OPDS feeds are XML documents based on the Atom format:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<feed xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom"
      xmlns:opds="http://opds-spec.org/2010/catalog">

              rel="alternate"
              type="application/epub+zip"
              length="1234567"/>
    </entry>
</feed>
```

## E-Reader Integration

1. User adds FicHub's OPDS URL to their e-reader
2. E-reader fetches the root catalog
3. User browses categories
4. User selects a story
5. E-reader downloads the EPUB
6. Story appears in the library

## Authentication

Some features (like shelves) require authentication via bearer token:

```
Authorization: Bearer <OPDS_SHELF_TOKEN>
```

# The Complete Guide to FicHub's Tagging System

## Tag Resolution

When a user submits a tag, FicHub resolves it through three steps:

1. **Exact match**: Check if the tag name exists in the `tags` table
2. **Alias lookup**: Check if the name is an alias for an existing tag
3. **Create new**: If neither matches, create a new canonical tag

## Community Voting

Users can upvote or downvote tags:

- Upvote (+1): "This tag accurately describes the story"
- Downvote (-1): "This tag does not belong"

A PostgreSQL trigger automatically recalculates the aggregate score.

## Visibility Threshold

Tags with scores at or below the threshold (default: -3) are hidden:

```rust
pub fn is_hidden(score: i16, threshold: i16) -> bool {
    score <= threshold
}
```

## The Curator System

Curators can:
- Create aliases (map alternative names to canonical tags)
- Merge tags (combine duplicates)
- Delete tags (remove inappropriate or unused tags)
- Resolve flags (address user-submitted reports)

# The Complete Guide to FicHub's Caching System

## Two-Level Cache

FicHub uses two levels of caching:

1. **Database cache** (export_log table): Tracks which files have been generated
2. **Disk cache**: Stores the actual generated files

## Cache Path Structure

```
cache/
├── epub/
│   ├── abc/
│   │   ├── def/
│   │   │   └── abcdef/
│   │   │       └── hash123.epub
```

The url_id is split into 3-character directory chunks to prevent too many files in one directory.

## Cache Invalidation

When a story is updated:
1. The content hash changes
2. The version bump is incremented
3. Old cached files are stale (different hash)
4. New exports are generated with the new hash

## Hash Validation

When serving cached files, FicHub verifies the MD5 hash:

```rust
match crate::cache::disk::file_md5(&cache_path) {
    Ok(actual_hash) if actual_hash == hash => {
        // Hash matches — serve the file
    }
    _ => {
        // Hash mismatch — file may be corrupted
        return Json(json!({"err": -5, "msg": "hash mismatch"}));
    }
}
```

# The Complete Guide to FicHub's Error Handling

## Error Type Hierarchy

```
AppError
├── BadRequest(400) — invalid input
├── RateLimited(429) — too many requests
├── NotFound(404) — resource not found
├── Internal(500) — unexpected errors
├── ScrapeError(502) — external service failure
├── ExportError(500) — file generation failure
├── Database(500) — database errors
└── CacheError(500) — cache errors
```

## Automatic Conversions

```rust
impl From<sqlx::Error> for AppError {
    fn from(err: sqlx::Error) -> Self {
        AppError::Database(err.to_string())
    }
}
```

## The ? Operator

```rust
// This single line can:
// 1. Execute the database query
// 2. If it fails, convert sqlx::Error to AppError
// 3. Return the AppError from the function
let row = queries::get_fic_info(&state.db, "abc123").await?;
```

## Error Information Leakage

Internal errors are logged but not sent to users:

```rust
AppError::Internal(msg) => {
    tracing::error!("Internal error: {}", msg);  // Logged
    (StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR,
     json!({"err": -1, "msg": "internal error"}))  // Generic message
}
```

# The Complete Guide to FicHub's Security

## SQL Injection Prevention

Always use parameterized queries:

```rust
// SAFE
sqlx::query("SELECT * FROM fic_info WHERE id = $1")
    .bind(user_input)
    .fetch_one(&pool)

// NEVER
format!("SELECT * FROM fic_info WHERE id = '{}'", user_input)
```

## XSS Prevention

Escape HTML in user-generated content:

```rust
fn escape_html(s: &str) -> String {
    s.replace('&', "&amp;")
        .replace('<', "&lt;")
        .replace('>', "&gt;")
        .replace('"', "&quot;")
        .replace('\'', "&#39;")
}
```

## Rate Limiting

The token bucket algorithm prevents abuse.

## Error Information Leakage

Internal errors are logged but not sent to users.

## Cache Hash Validation

Download URLs include MD5 hashes to prevent unauthorized access.

# The Complete Guide to FicHub's Troubleshooting

## Common Issues

### Database Connection Errors

```
Failed to connect to database
```

Solutions:
1. Check PostgreSQL is running: `systemctl status postgresql`
2. Verify connection string: `psql $DATABASE_URL`
3. Check firewall rules

### Redis Connection Errors

```
Failed to connect to Redis
```

Solutions:
1. Check Redis is running: `redis-cli ping`
2. Verify connection string

### Scraping Errors

```
ScrapeError: fic not found
```

Solutions:
1. Verify URL is correct
2. Check source site is accessible
3. Look for rate limiting

### Slow Requests

Solutions:
1. Check database query performance
2. Verify indexes are being used
3. Check network latency
4. Increase cache hit rate

# Understanding Rust's Ownership in FicHub

## Why Ownership Matters

Rust's ownership system is unique among programming languages. It ensures memory safety without a garbage collector. In FicHub, ownership is critical for several reasons:

### Shared State

The `AppState` struct is shared across all request handlers:

```rust
let state = Arc::new(AppState {
    config: config.clone(),
    db: db_pool,
    redis: redis_conn,
    http_client,
    scraper_registry,
    cache_semaphores: Arc::new(tokio::sync::Mutex::new(std::collections::HashMap::new())),
    rate_limiter: Box::new(rate_limiter),
    recommender_engine,
    collection_worker,
});
```

The `Arc` wrapper allows multiple handlers to share ownership of the same state. Without `Arc`, each handler would need its own copy, which would be wasteful and incorrect.

### Move Semantics

When a value is "moved," the original variable becomes invalid:

```rust
let config = Config::from_env();
let state = Arc::new(AppState { config: config, ... });
// config is no longer valid here — it was moved into AppState
```

This prevents accidental use of a value after it has been transferred.

### Borrowing

References allow you to use a value without taking ownership:

```rust
fn print_fic_info(fic: &FicInfo) {
    println!("Title: {}", fic.title);
}
// fic is still valid after this function call
```

### Lifetimes

Lifetimes ensure that references do not outlive the data they point to:

```rust
fn get_author<'a>(fic: &'a FicInfo) -> &'a str {
    &fic.author
}
```

The `'a` lifetime annotation says "the returned reference lives as long as the input reference."

## Ownership in Async Code

Async code complicates ownership because tasks can be suspended and resumed:

```rust
async fn process_fic(state: Arc<AppState>, url: String) {
    // state is moved into this async block
    // url is moved into this async block
    let meta = state.scraper_registry.lookup(&state.http_client, &url).await;
    // The await point might suspend this task
    // state and url must still be valid when the task resumes
}
```

The `Arc` ensures that `AppState` is shared safely across await points.

## Memory Safety Guarantees

Rust's ownership system prevents:
1. **Use-after-free**: Accessing memory that has been freed
2. **Double-free**: Freeing the same memory twice
3. **Data races**: Multiple threads accessing the same data simultaneously
4. **Null pointer dereferences**: Accessing a null pointer
5. **Buffer overflows**: Writing beyond the end of an array

# Understanding Concurrency in FicHub

## The Tokio Runtime

FicHub uses the Tokio runtime for async operations. Tokio provides:

### Task Scheduling

```rust
// Spawn a background task
tokio::spawn(async move {
    process_background_job(job).await;
});
```

### I/O Operations

```rust
// Non-blocking file read
let data = tokio::fs::read(&path).await?;

// Non-blocking network request
let response = reqwest::get(url).await?;
```

### Timers

```rust
// Sleep without blocking
tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_secs(1)).await;
```

### Channels

```rust
// Communication between tasks
let (tx, rx) = tokio::sync::mpsc::channel(100);
tx.send(message).await?;
let received = rx.recv().await?;
```

## Mutex vs. RwLock

FicHub uses different synchronization primitives for different purposes:

### Mutex (for semaphores)

```rust
pub type CacheSemaphores = Arc<Mutex<HashMap<(String, EType), Arc<Semaphore>>>>;
```

Mutex provides exclusive access. Only one task can hold the lock at a time.

### RwLock (for datacenter IPs)

```rust
datacenter_ips: Arc<RwLock<HashSet<IpAddr>>>,
```

RwLock allows multiple concurrent readers but exclusive writers. This is perfect for the datacenter IP list, which is read frequently but updated rarely.

### Atomic Operations (for rate limiter)

```rust
pub struct PerSiteRateLimiter {
    last_request: AtomicI64,
    delay_secs: u64,
}
```

Atomic operations are lock-free and very fast. They are used for the rate limiter's timestamp tracking.

## Deadlock Prevention

Deadlocks occur when two tasks are waiting for each other:

```rust
// Task 1: Lock A, then lock B
// Task 2: Lock B, then lock A
// → Deadlock!
```

FicHub avoids deadlocks by:
1. Always acquiring locks in the same order
2. Holding locks for the shortest possible time
3. Using `try_lock` where appropriate

# Understanding Error Propagation in FicHub

## The ? Operator

The `?` operator is Rust's primary error propagation mechanism:

```rust
async fn epub_handler(...) -> Result<Json<Value>, AppError> {
    let scraper = state.scraper_registry.find_scraper(query)
        .ok_or_else(|| AppError::BadRequest(-5, "unsupported URL".into()))?;

    let meta = scraper.lookup(&state.http_client, query).await
        .map_err(|e| AppError::ScrapeError(e.to_string()))?;

    queries::upsert_fic_info(&state.db, &fic_info_row).await?;

    // ... more operations with ?
}
```

Each `?` does three things:
1. Checks if the result is an error
2. If error, converts it using `From` trait
3. Returns the error from the function

## Error Conversion Chain

```
sqlx::Error → AppError::Database
redis::RedisError → AppError::CacheError
reqwest::Error → AppError::ScrapeError
std::io::Error → AppError::Internal
serde_json::Error → AppError::Internal
```

## Custom Error Types

FicHub's `AppError` enum is carefully designed:

```rust
pub enum AppError {
    BadRequest(i32, String),    // Client error with code
    RateLimited(u64),           // Rate limit with retry time
    NotFound(String),           // Resource not found
    Internal(String),           // Server error
    ScrapeError(String),        // External service error
    ExportError(String),        // File generation error
    Database(String),           // Database error
    CacheError(String),         // Cache error
}
```

Each variant maps to a specific HTTP status code and provides appropriate information.

# Understanding Database Design in FicHub

## Normalization

FicHub's database is well-normalized:

### First Normal Form (1NF)
- Each column contains atomic values
- No repeating groups

### Second Normal Form (2NF)
- All non-key columns depend on the entire primary key
- Example: `fic_tags` has composite PK `(url_id, tag_id)`, and `score` depends on both

### Third Normal Form (3NF)
- No transitive dependencies
- Example: Tag types are in a separate `tag_types` table, not embedded in `tags`

## Index Strategy

FicHub uses indexes strategically:

### Primary Key Indexes
```sql
fic_info(id)           -- Primary key, automatically indexed
tags(id)               -- Primary key
fic_tags(url_id, tag_id) -- Composite primary key
```

### Secondary Indexes
```sql
fic_info(text_search)   -- GIN index for full-text search
fic_tags(url_id)        -- For tag queries by story
fic_tags(tag_id)        -- For story queries by tag
fic_bookmarks(url_id)   -- For bookmark queries
fic_bookmarks(user_hash) -- For user favourite queries
```

### When to Add Indexes
- Columns used in WHERE clauses
- Columns used in JOIN conditions
- Columns used in ORDER BY
- Columns with high cardinality (many distinct values)

## Query Optimization

### Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM fic_info
WHERE text_search @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'harry potter')
ORDER BY ts_rank(text_search, plainto_tsquery('english', 'harry potter')) DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

### Avoid SELECT *

```sql
-- BAD
SELECT * FROM fic_info WHERE id = $1;

-- GOOD (if you only need title and author)
SELECT title, author FROM fic_info WHERE id = $1;
```

### Use Batch Queries

```rust
// BAD: N+1
for fic in &fics {
    let tags = get_tags(&pool, &fic.id).await?;
}

// GOOD: Batch
let url_ids: Vec<&str> = fics.iter().map(|f| f.id.as_str()).collect();
let all_tags = sqlx::query("SELECT * FROM fic_tags WHERE url_id = ANY($1)")
    .bind(&url_ids)
    .fetch_all(&pool)
    .await?;
```

# Understanding Web Scraping Ethics

## robots.txt

Many websites have a `robots.txt` file that tells scrapers which pages they can access:

```
User-agent: *
Disallow: /admin/
Disallow: /private/
```

FicHub respects these rules and identifies itself with a clear User-Agent.

## Rate Limiting

FicHub rate-limits its scraping to be a good citizen:

- AO3: 1 request per 2 seconds
- FF.net: 1 request per 5 seconds
- XenForo: 1 request per 3 seconds

## Caching

FicHub caches scraped data to minimize requests to source sites.

## User-Agent

FicHub identifies itself clearly:

```rust
.header("User-Agent", "fichub.net/0.1.0")
```

This allows website operators to contact FicHub if there are issues.

# Understanding the Export Pipeline

## The Complete Flow

```
1. User provides URL
   ↓
2. ScraperRegistry finds the right scraper
   ↓
3. Scraper.lookup() fetches metadata
   ↓
4. Metadata is stored in fic_info table
   ↓
5. Tags are auto-populated from scraper
   ↓
6. Blacklists are checked
   ↓
7. Cache is checked (export_log table)
   ↓
8. If cache miss:
   a. Acquire semaphore
   b. Double-check cache
   c. Fetch chapters
   d. Generate EPUB
   e. Cache EPUB on disk
   f. Record in export_log
   g. Generate HTML bundle
   h. Cache HTML on disk
   i. Record HTML in export_log
   ↓
9. Return download links
```

## Error Handling in the Pipeline

Each step can fail, and errors are propagated:

```rust
// Step 3: Scraper might fail
let meta = scraper.lookup(&state.http_client, query).await
    .map_err(|e| AppError::ScrapeError(e.to_string()))?;

// Step 4: Database might fail
queries::upsert_fic_info(&state.db, &fic_info_row).await?;

// Step 8c: Chapter fetching might fail
let chapters = scraper.fetch_chapters(&state.http_client, &meta).await
    .map_err(|e| AppError::ScrapeError(e.to_string()))?;

// Step 8d: EPUB generation might fail
let (epub_path, hash) = export::epub::create_epub(&meta, &chapters, &state.config.tmp_dir)
    .await
    .map_err(|e| AppError::ExportError(e.to_string()))?;
```

## Concurrency Control

The semaphore prevents duplicate exports:

```rust
let sem = cache::get_export_semaphore(&state.cache_semaphores, &meta.url_id, &EType::Epub).await;
let _permit = sem.acquire().await.map_err(|e| AppError::Internal(e.to_string()))?;
```

Only one task can generate an EPUB for a given story at a time.

# Understanding the Recommendation Algorithm

## Collaborative Filtering

The core algorithm:

1. **Find similar users**: Users who favourited the same stories
2. **Find their other favourites**: What else did they like?
3. **Count co-occurrences**: How many users liked both stories?
4. **Compute Jaccard similarity**: How similar are the stories?
5. **Blend with tag-based scores**: For stories with few favouriters
6. **Apply community boost**: User votes affect ranking

## The Math

### Jaccard Similarity

```
J(A, B) = |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|
```

Where:
- A = set of users who favourited story A
- B = set of users who favourited story B
- A ∩ B = users who favourited both
- A ∪ B = users who favourited either

### Score Blending

```
weight = min(1.0, favouriter_count / 5.0)
final = collab * weight + tag * (1.0 - weight)
```

### Community Boost

```
boost = 1.0 + gamma * ln(1 + max(0, net_votes))
final *= boost
```

## Performance

The recommendation engine is optimized:

1. **Precomputed cache**: Popular stories have recommendations precomputed
2. **Index usage**: Co-occurrence queries use composite indexes
3. **Batch processing**: The collection worker processes items efficiently
4. **Rate limiting**: Per-site rate limits prevent overwhelming source sites

# Understanding the Search System

## Full-Text Search

PostgreSQL's FTS is powerful:

### Tokenization
Breaking text into words: "Harry Potter" → ["harry", "potter"]

### Stemming
Reducing words to root form: "running" → "run"

### Stop Word Removal
Ignoring common words: "the", "a", "is"

### Ranking
Computing relevance: ts_rank(text_search, query)

## The Search Pipeline

1. Parse query parameters
2. Build dynamic SQL with SearchQueryBuilder
3. Execute count query (for pagination)
4. Execute data query (for results)
5. Batch-fetch tags for all results
6. Build response with enriched data

## Tag Filtering

Three types of tag filters:

### Include All (AND)
```sql
EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fic_tags WHERE tag_name = 'Harry Potter')
AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fic_tags WHERE tag_name = 'Fluff')
```

### Exclude (NOT EXISTS)
```sql
NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fic_tags WHERE tag_name = 'Angst')
```

### Include Any (OR)
```sql
EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fic_tags WHERE tag_name IN ('Fluff', 'Hurt/Comfort'))
```

# Understanding the OPDS Catalog

## What is OPDS?

OPDS (Open Publication Distribution System) is a standard for e-book distribution. It allows e-readers to browse and download books.

## Feed Structure

OPDS feeds are Atom XML with extensions:

```xml
<feed xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom"
      xmlns:opds="http://opds-spec.org/2010/catalog">
    <title>FicHub Catalog</title>
    <entry>
        <title>My Story</title>
        <link href="/cache/epub/abc123" type="application/epub+zip"/>
    </entry>
</feed>
```

## E-Reader Integration

1. Add FicHub's OPDS URL to e-reader
2. Browse categories (New, Popular, Tags)
3. Select a story
4. Download EPUB
5. Read!

## Authentication

Some features require a bearer token:

```
Authorization: Bearer <token>
```

---

# Understanding the Tagging System

## Tag Resolution

Three-step process:

1. **Exact match**: Check tags table
2. **Alias lookup**: Check tag_aliases table
3. **Create new**: Insert into tags table

## Community Voting

Users vote on tag accuracy:

- Upvote (+1): Tag is accurate
- Downvote (-1): Tag is inaccurate

A PostgreSQL trigger automatically recalculates scores.

## Visibility

Tags with scores at or below the threshold are hidden:

```rust
pub fn is_hidden(score: i16, threshold: i16) -> bool {
    score <= threshold
}
```

## Curator System

Curators can:
- Create aliases
- Merge tags
- Delete tags
- Resolve flags

---

# Understanding the Caching System

## Two-Level Cache

1. **Database cache** (export_log): Tracks generated files
2. **Disk cache**: Stores actual files

## Cache Path Structure

```
cache/<etype>/<prefix1>/<prefix2>/<prefix3>/<url_id>/<hash><suffix>
```

The url_id is split into 3-character chunks to prevent directory overcrowding.

## Cache Invalidation

When a story is updated:
1. Content hash changes
2. Version bump increments
3. Old cached files are stale
4. New exports are generated

## Hash Validation

Download URLs include MD5 hashes for integrity verification.

---

# Understanding the Rate Limiting System

## Token Bucket Algorithm

Two buckets:

### Global Bucket
- Capacity: 150 tokens
- Flow: 30 tokens/second
- Prevents server overload

### Per-IP Bucket
- Capacity: 30 tokens
- Flow: ~0.12 tokens/second
- Prevents individual abuse

## Lua Script

Runs atomically in Redis:

```lua
local value = tonumber(redis.call('HMGET', key, 'value')[1])
local elapsed = now - last_drain
local new_tokens = math.min(capacity, value + elapsed * flow)
if new_tokens >= requested then
    redis.call('HMSET', key, 'value', new_tokens - requested)
    return -1
else
    return (requested - new_tokens) / flow
end
```

## Failure Penalty

Failed requests consume extra tokens (1.5 instead of 1).

```rust
pub enum AppError {
    BadRequest(i32, String),    // Client error
    RateLimited(u64),           // Rate limit
    NotFound(String),           // Not found
    Internal(String),           // Server error
    ScrapeError(String),        // External service
    ExportError(String),        // File generation
    Database(String),           // Database
    CacheError(String),         // Cache
}
```

## Automatic Conversions

```rust
impl From<sqlx::Error> for AppError { ... }
impl From<redis::RedisError> for AppError { ... }
impl From<reqwest::Error> for AppError { ... }
```

## The ? Operator

Propagates errors automatically:

```rust

```

# Understanding the Security Model

## SQL Injection Prevention

Always use parameterized queries:

```rust
sqlx::query("SELECT * FROM fic_info WHERE id = $1")
    .bind(user_input)
    .fetch_one(&pool)
```

## XSS Prevention

Escape HTML in user content:

```rust
fn escape_html(s: &str) -> String {
    s.replace('&', "&amp;")
        .replace('<', "&lt;")
        .replace('>', "&gt;")
}
```

## Rate Limiting

Token bucket algorithm prevents abuse.

## Error Information Leakage

Internal errors are logged but not sent to users.

## Cache Hash Validation

Download URLs include MD5 hashes.

# The Complete Guide to FicHub's Server Initialization

## Step-by-Step Server Startup

When you run `cargo run`, here is exactly what happens:

### Phase 1: Environment Setup

```rust
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    dotenvy::dotenv().ok();
```

The `#[tokio::main]` attribute transforms our async main function into a synchronous one that creates a Tokio runtime and runs the async code inside it. This is equivalent to:

```rust
fn main() {
    tokio::runtime::Builder::new_multi_thread()
        .enable_all()
        .build()
        .unwrap()
        .block_on(async {
            // Our async main code here
        });
}
```

The `dotenvy::dotenv().ok()` loads environment variables from a `.env` file if it exists. The `.ok()` converts the Result to Option, silently ignoring errors.

### Phase 2: Logging Setup

```rust
    tracing_subscriber::fmt()
        .with_env_filter(
            tracing_subscriber::EnvFilter::try_from_default_env()
                .unwrap_or_else(|_| tracing_subscriber::EnvFilter::new("info,fichub=debug")),
        )
        .init();
```

This configures the logging system:
1. `fmt()` creates a human-readable text formatter
2. `with_env_filter()` reads the `RUST_LOG` environment variable
3. If `RUST_LOG` is not set, defaults to showing INFO for everything and DEBUG for fichub
4. `.init()` starts the logging system

### Phase 3: Configuration Loading

```rust
    let config = config::Config::from_env();
    tracing::info!("Starting fichub-rs server on port {}", config.app_port);
```

Loads all configuration from environment variables. Panics if required variables are missing.

### Phase 4: Database Connection

```rust
    let db_pool = db::init_pool(&config.database_url)
        .await
        .expect("Failed to connect to database");
```

Creates a connection pool with 20 max connections and runs pending migrations.

### Phase 5: Redis Connection

```rust
    let redis_client = redis::Client::open(config.redis_url.as_str())
        .expect("Invalid Redis URL");
    let redis_conn = redis_client.get_multiplexed_async_connection()
        .await
        .expect("Failed to connect to Redis");
```

Creates a multiplexed Redis connection.

### Phase 6: HTTP Client

```rust
    let http_client = reqwest::Client::builder()
        .user_agent("fichub.net/0.1.0")
        .timeout(std::time::Duration::from_secs(30))
        .build()
        .expect("Failed to build HTTP client");
```

Creates an HTTP client with User-Agent and timeout.

### Phase 7: Scraper Registry

```rust
    let scraper_registry = Arc::new(ScraperRegistry::new());
    tracing::info!("Registered {} scrapers", scraper_registry.scraper_count());
```

Creates all 6 site scrapers.

### Phase 8: Rate Limiter

```rust
    let rate_limiter = limiter::redis_bucket::RedisBucketLimiter::new(
        redis_conn.clone(),
        config.dynamic_rate_limit,
    )
    .await
    .expect("Failed to initialize rate limiter");
```

Creates the rate limiter and loads the Lua script into Redis.

### Phase 9: Datacenter IPs

```rust
    if !config.ip_tag_sources.is_empty() {
        rate_limiter.load_datacenter_ips(&config.ip_tag_sources).await;
    }
```

Loads datacenter IP lists if configured.

### Phase 10: Recommendation Engine

```rust
    let recommender_engine = RecommendationEngine::new(db_pool.clone());
```

Creates the recommendation engine.

### Phase 11: Collection Worker

```rust
    let collection_worker = CollectionWorker::new(
        db_pool.clone(),
        redis_conn.clone(),
        http_client.clone(),
        config.clone(),
        scraper_registry.clone(),
    );
```

Creates the background collection worker.

### Phase 12: Bundle State

```rust
    let state = Arc::new(AppState {
        config: config.clone(),
        db: db_pool,
        redis: redis_conn,
        http_client,
        scraper_registry,
        cache_semaphores: Arc::new(tokio::sync::Mutex::new(std::collections::HashMap::new())),
        rate_limiter: Box::new(rate_limiter),
        recommender_engine,
        collection_worker,
    });
```

Bundles everything into AppState.

### Phase 13: Build Router

```rust
    let app = build_router(state).await;
```

Builds the Axum router with all routes and middleware.

### Phase 14: Start Server

```rust
    let addr = format!("0.0.0.0:{}", config.app_port);
    tracing::info!("Listening on {}", addr);
    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind(&addr)
        .await
        .expect("Failed to bind to address");
    axum::serve(
        listener,
        app.into_make_service_with_connect_info::<std::net::SocketAddr>(),
    )
    .await
    .expect("Server error");
```

Binds to the port and starts serving requests.

# The Complete Guide to FicHub's Route Handling

## Route Definitions

The router defines all API endpoints:

```rust
Router::new()
    .route("/api/", get(routes::api_docs::api_docs_handler))
    .route("/api/v0/epub", get(routes::export::epub_handler))
    .route("/api/v0/meta", get(routes::meta::meta_handler))
    .route("/api/v0/remote", get(remote_handler))
    .route("/cache/{etype}/{url_id}/{fname}", get(routes::cache_download::download_with_hash))
    .route("/cache/{etype}/{url_id}", get(routes::cache_download::download_or_export))
    .route("/api/v0/recommendations", get(crate::recommender::routes::recommendations_handler))
    .route("/api/v0/recommendations/suggest", axum::routing::post(crate::recommender::routes::suggest_handler))
    .route("/api/v0/recommendations/vote", axum::routing::post(crate::recommender::routes::vote_handler))
    .route("/api/v0/recommendations/votes", get(crate::recommender::routes::votes_handler))
    .route("/api/v0/tags/submit", axum::routing::post(crate::tags::routes::submit_tag))
    .route("/api/v0/tags/vote", axum::routing::post(crate::tags::routes::vote_tag))
    .route("/api/v0/tags/flag", axum::routing::post(crate::tags::routes::flag_tag))
    .route("/api/v0/tags", get(crate::tags::routes::get_tags))
    .route("/api/v0/curator/alias", axum::routing::post(crate::tags::curator::create_alias))
    .route("/api/v0/curator/merge", axum::routing::post(crate::tags::curator::merge_tags))
    .route("/api/v0/curator/tags/{id}", axum::routing::delete(crate::tags::curator::delete_tag))
    .route("/api/v0/curator/flags", get(crate::tags::curator::list_flags))
    .route("/api/v0/curator/flags/{id}/resolve", axum::routing::post(crate::tags::curator::resolve_flag))
    .route("/api/v0/search", get(crate::search::routes::search_handler))
    .route("/opds", get(crate::routes::opds::feeds::root_catalog))
    .route("/opds/new", get(crate::routes::opds::feeds::recent_feed))
    .route("/opds/popular", get(crate::routes::opds::feeds::popular_feed))
    .route("/opds/tags", get(crate::routes::opds::tags::tag_types))
    .route("/opds/tags/{type_id}", get(crate::routes::opds::tags::tags_by_type))
    .route("/opds/tags/{type_id}/{tag_name}", get(crate::routes::opds::tags::fics_by_tag))
    .route("/opds/authors", get(crate::routes::opds::authors::author_list))
    .route("/opds/recommendations/popular", get(crate::routes::opds::recommendations::popular_recommendations))
    .route("/opds/recommendations", get(crate::routes::opds::recommendations::fic_recommendations))
    .route("/opds/search", get(crate::routes::opds::search::search_feed))
    .route("/opds/shelves", get(crate::routes::opds::shelves::shelf_list))
    .route("/opds/shelf/{shelf_id}", get(crate::routes::opds::shelves::shelf_contents))
    .route("/legacy/epub_export", get(redirect_to_root))
    .route("/fic/{url_id}", get(redirect_to_root))
    .route("/changes", get(redirect_to_root))
    .route("/popular/", get(redirect_to_root))
    .fallback_service(
        ServeDir::new(&frontend_dir)
            .append_index_html_on_directories(true)
            .fallback(ServeFile::new(frontend_dir.join("index.html"))),
    )
    .layer(TraceLayer::new_for_http())
    .layer(CorsLayer::permissive())
    .with_state(state)
```

## Route Groups

### API Routes
- `/api/` — API documentation
- `/api/v0/epub` — Export story as EPUB
- `/api/v0/meta` — Get story metadata
- `/api/v0/remote` — Get client IP info
- `/api/v0/search` — Advanced search
- `/api/v0/tags` — Tag operations
- `/api/v0/recommendations` — Recommendation operations
- `/api/v0/curator` — Curator operations

### Cache Routes
- `/cache/{etype}/{url_id}/{fname}` — Direct download with hash
- `/cache/{etype}/{url_id}` — Export and download

### OPDS Routes
- `/opds` — Root catalog
- `/opds/new` — Recently added
- `/opds/popular` — Popular stories
- `/opds/tags` — Browse by tag
- `/opds/authors` — Browse by author
- `/opds/search` — Search catalog
- `/opds/shelves` — User shelves

### Legacy Routes
- `/legacy/epub_export` — Redirect to frontend
- `/fic/{url_id}` — Redirect to frontend
- `/changes` — Redirect to frontend
- `/popular/` — Redirect to frontend

## Handler Signatures

Every handler follows this pattern:

```rust
pub async fn handler_name(
    State(state): State<Arc<AppState>>,
    // Optional extractors:
    Query(params): Query<ParamType>,
    Path((param1, param2)): Path<(Type1, Type2)>,
    ConnectInfo(remote): ConnectInfo<SocketAddr>,
    Json(body): Json<BodyType>,
) -> Result<Json<Value>, AppError> {
    // Handler logic
}
```


Blocks automated requests (bots).

```rust
        .ok_or_else(|| AppError::BadRequest(-5, format!("unsupported URL: {}", query)))?;
```

Finds the appropriate scraper for the URL.

```rust
    let meta = scraper.lookup(&state.http_client, query).await
        .map_err(|e| AppError::ScrapeError(e.to_string()))?;
```

Fetches metadata from the source site.


Records how long the metadata fetch took.

```rust
    let fic_info_row = FicInfo {
        id: meta.url_id.clone(),
        created: None,
        updated: None,

        author: meta.author.clone(),
        // ... more fields

```

Stores the metadata in the database.

```rust
    if let Ok(extracted_tags) = scraper.extract_tags(&state.http_client, query).await {
        for tag in &extracted_tags {
            if let Ok(resolution) = crate::tags::resolve::resolve_tag(
                &state.db, &tag.name, tag.tag_type_id,
            ).await {
                let _ = queries::upsert_fic_tag(
                    &state.db, &meta.url_id, resolution.tag_id,
                    &std::net::IpAddr::V4(std::net::Ipv4Addr::UNSPECIFIED),
                ).await;
            }
        }
    }
```

Auto-populates tags from the scraper.

```rust
    let fic_blacklist = queries::check_fic_blacklist(&state.db, &meta.url_id).await?;
    if !fic_blacklist.is_empty() {
        if fic_blacklist.iter().any(|b| b.reason == 6) {
            return Ok(build_metadata_response(&meta, &[], &state.config.export_version, None, true));
        }
        if fic_blacklist.iter().any(|b| b.reason == 5 || b.reason == 7 || b.reason == 8) {
            return Ok(Json(json!({"err": -7, "msg": "fic is blacklisted", "q": query})));
        }
    }
```

Checks blacklists. Greylisted fics show metadata but no downloads. Hard blacklisted fics return an error.

```rust
    let version_bump = queries::get_fic_version_bump(&state.db, &meta.url_id).await?.unwrap_or(0);
    let version = state.config.export_version + version_bump;
```

Computes the cache version.

```rust
    let input_hash = meta.content_hash.clone().unwrap_or_else(|| "upstream".to_string());
    let cached = queries::find_export_log(&state.db, &meta.url_id, version, "epub", &input_hash).await?;
```

Checks if the export is already cached.

```rust
    if let Some(export_log) = cached {
        let epub_hash = &export_log.export_hash;

            "err": 0,

            // ...
        })));
    }
```

If cached, returns immediately.

```rust
    let sem = cache::get_export_semaphore(&state.cache_semaphores, &meta.url_id, &EType::Epub).await;
    let _permit = sem.acquire().await.map_err(|e| AppError::Internal(e.to_string()))?;
```

Acquires the semaphore to prevent duplicate exports.

```rust
    let cached = queries::find_export_log(&state.db, &meta.url_id, version, "epub", &input_hash).await?;
```

```rust
        "meta": build_meta_json(&meta),
        "hashes": hashes,
        "urls": urls,
        "epub_url": urls.get("epub"),
        "html_url": urls.get("html"),
        "mobi_url": urls.get("mobi"),
        "pdf_url": urls.get("pdf"),
        "notes": notes,
    })))
}
```

Returns the final response.
